utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Good morning. Could you call the case for hearing, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Case number IT-01-42-T, the Prosecutor versus Pavle Strugar.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Ms. Somers.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. President. Good morning, Your Honours. I would just like to take a preliminary introduction moment to let the Court know to my left, Ms. Lamb, my colleague, will be leading the evidence this morning, and to my right, Ms. Andrea Matacic, a research officer and lawyer, will also be present this session. The first witness for the Prosecution this morning, is Ms. Ljerka Alajbeg.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It was Ms. Martin, was it?

utterances.speaker: MS. LAMB
utterances.text: Ms. Lamb.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Lamb. I beg your pardon, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, with your leave, I would like to address you for a moment. Your Honour, may I say a few words?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, indeed, Mr. Petrovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. Before today's witness enters the courtroom, I would like to raise an issue which seems important to me, in view of the contents of the testimony of this witness. From the statement we received, relating to Ljerka Alajbeg, we will see that this witness will testify about two main points. The first of these is when, in the witness's opinion, Croatia acquired the epithets of an independent state and became a subject of international law; and the second issue which arises from this is the question of the existence or non-existence of an international armed conflict, which is of importance for the application of appropriate instruments, on the basis of which our client has been charged. What concerns me, and what I would like to hear your standpoint on is the following: This witness will testify about two legal issues. These two legal issues are contained in the appropriate counts of the indictment, and they are something that in our view is a legal question to be resolved by the Tribunal. In our jurisdiction, legal issues are solved by the Court. It is the Court that can decide whether an entity is an independent state, and as of which date, and whether there is an international armed conflict. If the Court requires assistance in clarifying either of these two issues, the parties to the proceedings, in our jurisdiction, have to bring in an expert who is able to give the Court information important for reaching this decision. Therefore, the expert can clarify certain points for the Court, and this expert has to have the required knowledge and information and has to be independent. The expert will give opinions in accordance with the rules of the profession and of scholarship. In this situation, we have a witness appearing here as a witness and not an expert, and this witness will testify about two legal issues and will give her own interpretation of these two legal issues. This witness cannot be considered to be independent. The principle that I have set out is something that is not peculiar to my own jurisdiction. Before this Tribunal, issues such as the existence or non-existence of an international armed conflict, the date of recognition of a certain entity as a subject of international law, these are points on which opinions have been given by experts in these areas. Let me just remind you of the Prosecutor versus Dokmanovic. In that case, both sides brought in experts who clarified the issue of the existence or non-existence of an international armed conflict. The same time period covered here was relevant and was discussed. Before this witness enters the courtroom and gives her testimony, the Defence raises an objection to this approach and to what is expected to be presented as information before this Bench, because the information we are expecting is supposed to be information that should be independent. It should be the result of something that is the result of professional knowledge and appropriate information. The witness who will be brought before you will testify about the circumstances of an international conflict and the independence of the state, and we believe that this witness is not independent, that this witness has an interest in this matter. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Petrovic, for raising two interesting questions. Ms. Somers.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. First and foremost, Mrs. Alajbeg is a fact witness who was involved in the process, and she will indicate to the Chamber what was done by the Croatian -- by the Republic of Croatia at the time and its reasoning. We understand fully that the legal issue of international armed conflict or not is a matter that is within the sound discretion or finding to be made by the Chamber. There is no attempt to interfere with the triers of fact. The Chamber is entitled to have the information as to what happened at the time, and I'm sure the Chamber recognises that there may always technically be mixed fact/expert witnesses. But this is a person who is indeed a player at the time of the event and will provide evidence to this Chamber of what happened, what the reasoning was, what the events were which triggered. Should the Chamber seek any further expert, dispassionate, disinterested opinion, the Prosecution is always happy to commission said. It is in our view, through a fact witness who, at the time, can explain the hows, whys, whens, and put in context the various events, documents, conferences, that are relevant for the Chamber's knowledge on this issue. It is with this purpose that she is brought, and we believe she is the best person to present these facts to the Chamber. There is ample precedent in this institution for persons who have sat at the time in positions or have played roles in shaping the events that are the crux of the background to the conflict. I bring to the Chamber's attention Mr. Stjepan Kljuc who was the Bosnian Croat member of the presidency, who gave evidence in the Kordic case, President Stipe Mesic, president of Croatia, who has given evidence in the Milosevic case. It is not an unusual or unexceptional phenomenon to bring those persons before the Chamber who are best placed to give the information needed. The Defence's position is without merit, and I might add, done beyond the 11th hour, but there is no merit to the position and we believe that this will be helpful to the Chamber. And again, should any additional evidence or type of proof be sought, upon the Chamber's direction we would be very happy to bring in an expert.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Somers. Mr. Petrovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I'll be very brief. This witness is not a fact witness. Why? This witness did not participate in any of the events that the documents mention. At the time of significance and relevant to the indictment, this witness was not in the Ministry of Foreign Affairs of the Republic of Croatia. She only joined the ministry in December 1991, which is a time after the time covered in the indictment. So that this witness is in no way directly connected to these events. This witness was not present when any of these documents were drawn up and was not present at any of the meetings that are mentioned here. So this is something that is completely outside the experience of this witness. And this is the reason for our objection to what we expect this witness to testify about before you today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Petrovic. And I thank both counsel for the clarity of their submissions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It should first be clear that the issues whether, Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. and if so, when, Croatia became an independent legal state, and whether, at the time relevant to the indictment, there was an international conflict, are questions of law, as Mr. Petrovic submits, which will be determined as matters of law by the Trial Chamber at the appropriate stage of the hearing. When each of those matters might have occurred, and whether they occurred, are questions that, while of, in the end, of a character which is one of law, each must be determined in light of the factual circumstances that led to those matters occurring, if it is the case that they occurred. The facts which will help the Tribunal to assess whether or not either of those matters has been established are matters that will come from witnesses as to facts and from various documents that were contemporaneous at the time, if those documents exist. They are matters which may properly be the subject of evidence led before this Chamber, with a view then to the Chamber assessing whether, in light of that factual evidence, there is established the critical legal issues. It is our view, Mr. Petrovic, whilst appreciating the importance and the very appropriateness of your submission, that we should hear the evidence of this witness, but please be assured that we well respect the concern that you have that the witness is speaking only as a witness of fact. The witness will not be speaking as an expert witness, so that the evidence given by the witness will be regarded by the Chamber merely as evidence of fact, and whether or not it helps the Prosecution in the establishment of those two critical issues are matters which we will have to weigh at the end of the day.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: If the witness could be called.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: If the witness could take the affirmation. Good morning.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Witness answered through interpreter].

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Please be seated.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Ms. Lamb.

utterances.speaker: MS. LAMB
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Witness, are you now seated comfortably and can you hear me?

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG
utterances.text: Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: MS. LAMB
utterances.text: Could you please state your name, your nationality, and date of birth for the record.

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG
utterances.text: My name is Ljerka Alajbeg. I was born on the 9th of April, 1946, in Zagreb. I am a Croat by nationality.

utterances.speaker: MS. LAMB
utterances.text: What is your current occupation?

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG
utterances.text: At present I'm the ambassador of the Republic of Croatia, to the Kingdom of Belgium, and to the Grand Duchy of Luxembourg.

utterances.speaker: MS. LAMB
utterances.text: For how long have you held this position?

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG
utterances.text: Two years now.

utterances.speaker: MS. LAMB
utterances.text: What did you do before that?

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG
utterances.text: Before that, I worked in the Ministry of Foreign Affairs of the Republic of Croatia. I am still an employee of the ministry. From 1991 up until the present.

utterances.speaker: MS. LAMB
utterances.text: And what was your function or title as an employee of the Croatian foreign ministry?

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG
utterances.text: From 1991, I worked in the international legal affairs office, first as a legal advisor, then as the chief, and then as the chief legal advisor of the Ministry of Foreign Affairs. In the meantime, I was the ministerial advisor in our embassy in Ottawa.

utterances.speaker: MS. LAMB
utterances.text: As chief legal advisor of the international law section, what was some of your responsibilities?

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG
utterances.text: There were very few of us in the ministry at the time. In 1991, there were only 50 employees there, and we had to do everything. The ministry was being set up at the time, and I worked on various international law affairs, ranging from giving my opinion, advice, to work on international treaties, and I worked on this very closely. I was very closely involved. We also had multilateral affairs, contacts with various international organisation. We also dealt in protocol. We did all kinds of work, because there were very few of us with some kind of experience. I was one of those who had some experience in the former Ministry of Foreign Affairs in Yugoslavia and at that time we helped introduce others to the job. So all my work was in the field of international law and international contacts.

utterances.speaker: MS. LAMB
utterances.text: Ms. Alajbeg, encompassed within the scope of those responsibilities, were you frequently called upon to advise on matters of treaty law application and to advise on issues of recognition pertaining to states? A yes or no answer would be sufficient.

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, certainly. The international law service always gave its opinion on every international treaty.

utterances.speaker: MS. LAMB
utterances.text: Thank you. Ms. Alajbeg, you commenced your foreign service career, however, as an employee of the Yugoslav federal Ministry of Foreign Affairs; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG
utterances.text: Speaking of my legal career, this began in the INA Naftaplin company, which was the largest company for petroleum and gas in Croatia and in the Yugoslavia of the time.

utterances.speaker: MS. LAMB
utterances.text: At what point did you first join the foreign service?

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG
utterances.text: In 1979, first on contract, when I was preparing to become a consul in Pittsburgh, in the USA, and then an advisor in the Yugoslav cultural centre. And on my return, I was given a permanent job, and as of that time I worked on international law affairs. This was my own wish, because of my legal background.

utterances.speaker: MS. LAMB
utterances.text: To clarify, Ms. Alajbeg: At that point, this was with the federal Ministry of Foreign Affairs in Belgrade; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG
utterances.text: Yes, correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. LAMB
utterances.text: So to perhaps summarise this, Ms. Alajbeg, if I am correct, you have almost 30 years of foreign ministry experience on matters of international law; yes or no?

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG
utterances.text: Not quite 30. I have 35 years of experience all together, and I would say I have 25 years of experience in international law matters. Although you know that diplomats are also sent abroad, and I had several appointments abroad at that time when I was not involved in international law affairs, but I was frequently consulted. So I kept in touch with this area throughout this time.

utterances.speaker: MS. LAMB
utterances.text: Ms. Alajbeg, I'm going to turn now to your whereabouts, where you were located professionally during 1991. Did you remain in Belgrade throughout 1991?

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG
utterances.text: Not all the time, because at the end of that year, I returned to Croatia, because I was received into the Ministry of Foreign Affairs of the Republic of Croatia. Before that, I put myself at the disposal of the Croatian government, because the Croatian government had called upon all those who originated from Croatia and were employed in the then federal administrative organs, and this included us who were in the Ministry of Foreign Affairs. I responded to that invitation and put myself at their disposal. There were a number of circumstances on which the time when we would be transferred depended. These were both objective and subjective circumstances. Some people had their own personal problems which they had to solve, and also objectively, the Republic of Croatia was looking for civil servants, and this is how we came to be transferred from the federal ministries to the Croatian ministries. In 1991, I spent most of the year in Belgrade physically, although my transfer began in the summer, when I put myself at the disposal of the Croatian government, until the end of the year, because there were still matters that I had to attend to, so I was actually in both places at once.

utterances.speaker: MS. LAMB
utterances.text: Mrs. Alajbeg, in order to provide you with some form of road map, this morning I will be leading your testimony around four separate factual questions. Firstly, we will examine the process of the dissolution of the SFRY and the emergence of the independent state of Croatia. I will then move to the recognition of Croatia by other states. I will next proceed to the degree of effectiveness of Croatian state organs. And finally, I will be examining documents which speak to the effective date of Croatian succession which have emerged subsequent to these events. Before commencing, however, I would request that all documents contained in Prosecution Exhibit -- in our Prosecution Exhibit binder, be entered into evidence, and assigned an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I take it, Ms. Lamb, these are the black binders that are before the members of the Chamber; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MS. LAMB
utterances.text: That is correct, Your Honour. And in the course of this examination, I would propose to refer to each of these documents by the tab numbers that appear before you also.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It's apparent from the nature of it that it may be convenient to treat the binder as one exhibit.

utterances.speaker: MS. LAMB
utterances.text: I would be much obliged, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: And there are then internal tab numbers that will serve to separately identify each document within the one exhibit. We should look forward to the possibility, just born out of cautious experience, that you in fact may not prove or may not use one or more of the particular documents. Could I suggest that at the end of the evidence of the witness, if there is one or if there are more than one document that has not been specifically dealt with, that they might then be removed from the bundle, so that they are left only with documents that have been properly dealt with.

utterances.speaker: MS. LAMB
utterances.text: I would be happy to advise on that, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: On that basis, and subject to that possibility, the black binder of exhibit documents will be received as an exhibit.

utterances.speaker: MS. LAMB
utterances.text: In that case, Mrs. Alajbeg --

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit number P20.

utterances.speaker: MS. LAMB
utterances.text: Mrs. Alajbeg, on this basis, I will then go firstly to the events of the 1991, and I would ask you to turn to the document contained in tab 1 of our Prosecution binder. Mrs. Alajbeg, I would ask you to look at this document, which bears the date 23 April 1991, and tell the Court whether or not you recognise it.

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG
utterances.text: If we're talking about the conclusions on political circumstances in the Republic of Croatia, yes, this is the document which can be found in the Official Gazette, the Official Gazette of Republic of Croatia, issue number 19, dated 23rd April 1991, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. LAMB
utterances.text: Could you now then, within that document, kindly turn to the document numbered within it, bearing paragraph number 589, and bearing the date 17th of April, 1991. And as you've mentioned, this is entitled "conclusions of the Croatian assembly." I would refer you in particular to paragraph 6 and 7 of these conclusions. They will be appearing on the screen in front of you. That would assist you as well. Briefly, what conclusions are contained in paragraph 7 of this document concerning the legitimacy of the SFRY presidency?

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG
utterances.text: This document, I have to give you a brief introduction. This document speaks of the state of affairs in the former state, the SFRY. The Republic of Croatia has reacted -- had reacted to those political state of affairs. This document is no exception. In item 7, it is established that the presidency of the SFRY was formed in an unconstitutional manner in terms of the representation of the Republic of Serbia and the autonomous regions in that state body, and the question of legitimacy is therefore rightfully raised. And the assembly of the Republic of Croatia asked that the constitutional court of Yugoslavia immediately issue a decision on that matter. So this is one of the reactions to the unconstitutional composition of the presidency of the then-Yugoslavia, because not everybody was represented in an adequate way.

utterances.speaker: MS. LAMB
utterances.text: And in paragraph 6, Mrs. Alajbeg, what conclusions are drawn, what statement is made as to the preferred future constitutional relationship between the Republic of Croatia and the then-SFRY?

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG
utterances.text: In paragraph 6, it says that the assembly of the Republic of Croatia considers it crucial to accelerate the process of disassociation from the present SFRY and the possible membership of the Republic of Croatia in a confederation of sovereign states and express its readiness to cooperate on an interparliamentary level in that process.

utterances.speaker: MS. LAMB
utterances.text: As a senior federal foreign ministry official, what overall observations did you make during this period concerning the functioning of the federal presidency? Can you give examples of how it appeared to function in this period? I'm not at this point referring to a particular place in any document.

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG
utterances.text: I must react to this "senior" official in the federal organs. At that time, I was just an official, an expert. I was not a political figure. I was not appointed as such. So I cannot give you any crucial political statements. However, as an expert who worked in the Ministry of Foreign Affairs, I obviously noticed the non-functioning thereof. Later on, we would see that the Croatian representative in the then-presidency of the SFRY was prevented from taking over his constitutional duty of president. It was obvious that the organs were not functioning properly, that there were -- that there was no constitutional order in place, and that we were facing a new situation in the then-state which would then end up in the dissolution of the state. The climate, the atmosphere in the federal bodies reflected that and the foreign ministry was no exception to that. As time went on, it became more and more obvious. Everybody was turned towards their own republic, and the joint organs stopped functioning already after that summer. Certain representatives of certain republics started abandoning federal bodies. I remember a group of our colleagues from Slovenia walking out and going back home. We from Croatia did it on an individual basis, and finally it turned out that even those colleagues who did not return did not have any work to do in this particular federal organ. There were also some other problems that we heard of. We were informed about the conclusions reached at various sessions of the then-federal bodies. There was a lot of discord, and this all reflected on our work in our body.

utterances.speaker: MS. LAMB
utterances.text: Mrs. Alajbeg, I'm now going to turn to events within Croatia itself in this period, and I would ask that you turn to tab 2 of the Prosecution Exhibit binder. And I refer at this point to the document dated the 2nd of May, 1991. I would ask you whether you recognise this document.

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG
utterances.text: Yes. This is a decision on calling a referendum, also published in the Official Gazette, issue 21. The date is 2nd May 1991.

utterances.speaker: MS. LAMB
utterances.text: Thank you. Within this document, could I please refer you to the document numbered 646. What is the title of this document and what subject matter does it refer to?

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG
utterances.text: Yes. This is decision to call a referendum. This was passed by the president of the Republic of Croatia. And this deals with the referendum which would raise two issues, two specific issues, that mentioned here.

utterances.speaker: MS. LAMB
utterances.text: Very briefly, what was this referendum to decide?

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG
utterances.text: In a nutshell, the referendum was supposed to answer the following questions. That is, the citizens of the Republic of Croatia were supposed to answer the following questions. The first one: Are you in favour of the Republic of Croatia remaining in Yugoslavia as a state or not?

utterances.speaker: MS. LAMB
utterances.text: Thank you. Mrs. Alajbeg, can you turn you now to tab 3 of our binder. Can you mention -- tell the Court whether you recognise this document, and if so, what do you recognise it as?

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG
utterances.text: Again, this is issue 24 of the Official Gazette, published on 27 May 1991.

utterances.speaker: MS. LAMB
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG
utterances.text: That is the document.

utterances.speaker: MS. LAMB
utterances.text: And the document contained therein, numbered 708, what is this document?

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG
utterances.text: This is a decision, a decision passed by the president of the Republic of Croatia after the referendum, which was held on 25th April 1991. The decision was passed on the 23rd of May, 1991.

utterances.speaker: MS. LAMB
utterances.text: And briefly --

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG
utterances.text: And in this decision, it says that -- what the results of the referendum are.

utterances.speaker: MS. LAMB
utterances.text: And what were the results of this referendum?

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG
utterances.text: The result was that the Republic of Croatia would not remain in Yugoslavia as a unified state, but that it would become an independent state which would be entitled to forming alliances with other independent states, independent republics.

utterances.speaker: MS. LAMB
utterances.text: Thank you. Mrs. Alajbeg, can you now turn to the document at tab 4 of the Prosecution binder. Do you recognise this document, and if so, what do you recognise it as?

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG
utterances.text: Official Gazette, issue number 31, dated 25 June 1991.

utterances.speaker: MS. LAMB
utterances.text: Document number 872 within this Gazette is what?

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG
utterances.text: This is the constitutional decision on the sovereignty and independence of the Republic of Croatia. The decision was passed by the parliament of the Republic of Croatia at its session held on 25th June 1991.

utterances.speaker: MS. LAMB
utterances.text: What is this constitutional decision colloquially referred to as?

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG
utterances.text: Pursuant to this constitutional decision, the parliament of the Republic of Croatia promulgated a Republic of Croatia as a sovereign and independent state.

utterances.speaker: MS. LAMB
utterances.text: Is this document frequently referred to, Mrs. Alajbeg, as the -- to as the Croatian declaration of independence?

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG
utterances.text: Yes. A corresponding declaration was also published in the same issue, so these two documents combined are considered the Croatian declaration of independence. Pursuant to this same decision, Croatia started a process of dissolution from other republics of the former Yugoslavia, and it also started the process aimed at international recognition.

utterances.speaker: MS. LAMB
utterances.text: What did you observe about the character of the relationship between the Croatian Republic and the republics of Yugoslavia and Montenegro around this time?

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG
utterances.text: The character of the relationship. It is a generally known fact that an aggression had been launched against the Republic of Croatia, and that this aggression started in 1991. All these documents are the result of the situation in which Croatia had already been invaded by foreign troops, troops that had come from other republics. I cannot talk about all the republics, of course. It goes without saying which republics those were.

utterances.speaker: MS. LAMB
utterances.text: Mrs. Alajbeg, are you aware of the response by the European communities to this observed increase in tensions between the various republics at this time?

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG
utterances.text: Of course. The international community realised that something was going on. They tried to preserve the former Yugoslavia in all sorts of ways. However, things had stopped functioning. Later on, it turned out that one of the ways by which to preserve Yugoslavia was the proposal by the international community for this decision, which is almost identical to the one that was passed on the same day in the parliament of Slovenia, for Slovenia. So the republics of Croatia and the Republic of Slovenia were working in sync, because they were attacked at the same time and they wanted both to gain their independence at the same time. The international community wanted the effect of both these decisions to be postponed by three months in order to preserve the former Yugoslavia. And this was done, and this was stipulated by a document, the so-called Brioni Declaration.

utterances.speaker: MS. LAMB
utterances.text: Mrs. Alajbeg, let us turn to that Brioni Declaration right now. It is found at tab 5 in the Prosecution binder. Could you summarise briefly who were the main participants within this so-called Brioni Declaration? I apologise. Perhaps firstly you could identify this document, which commences on the page bearing the ERN number 00570261. Does the text which you see in front of you on this page, is this the Brioni Declaration, to which you have just referred?

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG
utterances.text: Just a moment, please. Yes, this is dated 7 July 1991, and the title is "joint declaration."

utterances.speaker: MS. LAMB
utterances.text: Who were the participants within that process, as identified within the preambular provisions of that declaration?

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG
utterances.text: In the preamble of this declaration, it says that the participants -- the document is in English, so I will read it in English. The European Ministerial Troika [In English] With representatives of all parties directly concerned by the Yugoslav crisis.

utterances.speaker: MS. LAMB
utterances.text: Thank you. What impact did this declaration have upon the timing of the Croatian declaration of independence? What was -- in essence, what was agreed at Brioni with regard to the timing of the announcement of the Croatian declaration of independence?

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Basically, the effects thereof were suspended. Also, this served to introduce some measures and procedures which would help to resolve some discords. And the cessation of initial hostilities is also mentioned. Also, this serves to deal with some other practical issues and introduces the European Monitoring Mission.

utterances.speaker: MS. LAMB
utterances.text: Mrs. Alajbeg, what was the impact of the cumulative measures set up at Brioni? That is, did it appear to have the desired effect on the ground? Did it appear to bring about a rapprochement between the parties?

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG
utterances.text: The goal was to stop hostilities and for the army to withdraw and maybe to achieve some sort of agreement that would lead to the establishment of some sort of a union. At the beginning, Croatia was in favour of establishing a confederation that would comprise the former republics.

utterances.speaker: MS. LAMB
utterances.text: Mrs. Alajbeg, I apologise. The -- my question was in fact: What did you observe about the quality of the relationship in the aftermath of Brioni? Did you observe -- it is clear that the Brioni Declaration sought this result, but did it in fact achieve it? Did you observe any lessening in the tension between the parties?

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG
utterances.text: You're correct. On the contrary; tensions continued to grow.

utterances.speaker: MS. LAMB
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG
utterances.text: And immediately after that, we had a full-blown war.

utterances.speaker: MS. LAMB
utterances.text: Let us now turn to the relationship that existed between the belligerents within this armed conflict to which you have just described -- just referred. I refer you at this juncture to the document contained at tab number 6. In particular, I would refer you therein to the document bearing the date 8th of October, 1991, and the ERN number 01074963.

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG
utterances.text: 6. Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. LAMB
utterances.text: Mrs. Alajbeg, do you recognise that document, and if so, what do you recognise it to be?

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG
utterances.text: If I have the right document in front of me, then this is --

utterances.speaker: MS. LAMB
utterances.text: I apologise.

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG
utterances.text: I'm sorry. There is also a Croatian version, so I think I will rather read it in Croatian.

utterances.speaker: MS. LAMB
utterances.text: Yes. I'd be much obliged, Mrs. Alajbeg. And I apologise. The correct page number is in fact 01074958.

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG
utterances.text: Thank you very much. This is an initiative of the Assembly of the Republic of Montenegro, dated 8 October 1991.

utterances.speaker: MS. LAMB
utterances.text: Thank you. In the light of the Croatian Declaration of Independence to which we have just referred, what does paragraph 1 of this initiative acknowledge about the border between the two republics?

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG
utterances.text: In paragraph 1, the Assembly of the Republic of Montenegro, taking into consideration the decision of the Republic of Croatia to become a sovereign and independent state -- so this is clear what the Republic of Croatia wants. The assembly finds this decision to change the status of the border between the Republic of Montenegro and the Republic of Croatia. In this document, further on, it says that the state border remains, the land border remains what it is because this was in accordance with all the documents that were in effect within Yugoslavia, and it is emphasised that the land border should become a state border. And as for coast waters, which had been shared and where there had been no international border, this border had to be determined.

utterances.speaker: MS. LAMB
utterances.text: So if I understand you correctly, Mrs. Alajbeg, the border had issues of contention to be determined, but it was nevertheless acknowledged that in due course it would become an international border. Would that be the gist of your testimony?

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG
utterances.text: Yes. There was no dispute about any of the borders. It was confirmed that a land border, pursuant to the international law, would become a state border, whereas the border on the sea, which had never been determined between the former republics, had to be determined. So this document calls for the determination of this sea borders between the two newly formed states.

utterances.speaker: MS. LAMB
utterances.text: Mrs. Alajbeg, were armed hostilities ongoing between the Republic of Croatia and the Republic of Serbia and Montenegro around this state?

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG
utterances.text: The problem is that aggression on Croatia was also waged from the territory of Montenegro, not necessarily by Montenegrin bodies. But it is well known that the JNA also acted from the territory of Montenegro.

utterances.speaker: MS. LAMB
utterances.text: Mrs. Alajbeg, I would now ask you to turn to the document contained at tab number 7. Do you recognise this document, and if so, what as?

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG
utterances.text: Just a moment, please. This is a document published in the Official Gazette, number 53, of the 8th of October, 1991. It's called a decision, and the decision is also dated 8th of October, 1991. And it pertains to breaking the relations of public law between the then-republics, or rather, with the former state of SFRY.

utterances.speaker: MS. LAMB
utterances.text: Mrs. Alajbeg, to clarify: The document to which you have just referred, does it bear the number 1265? Just for the purposes of the record.

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. LAMB
utterances.text: Thank you. I would turn now to the document contained at tab 8. Do you recognise this document, and if so, what do you recognise it to be?

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG
utterances.text: Number 8, the Official Gazette, number 66, of the 9th of December, 1991.

utterances.speaker: MS. LAMB
utterances.text: Could you refer therein to the document numbered 1681.

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG
utterances.text: Yes. This is a conclusion.

utterances.speaker: MS. LAMB
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... What --

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG
utterances.text: This is a conclusion of the parliament of the Republic of Croatia, of the 8th of October, stating that on the 8th of October, Stjepan Mesic's function, as member and president of the Presidency of the former Socialist Federative Republic of Yugoslavia shall be terminated as of 8th October 1991.

utterances.speaker: MS. LAMB
utterances.text: Briefly, who is Stjepan Mesic and what position did he hold at this time?

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG
utterances.text: Stjepan Mesic was then a member of the Presidency of the SFRY, and he was the president of the Presidency. After the Brioni Declaration, he was --

utterances.speaker: MS. LAMB
utterances.text: Thank you. What date does this decision bear?

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG
utterances.text: The conclusion bears the date 5th of December, 1991.

utterances.speaker: MS. LAMB
utterances.text: Nevertheless, when -- at what date does this declaration purport to take effect?

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG
utterances.text: This is not stated in the conclusion itself, although it was published.

utterances.speaker: MS. LAMB
utterances.text: Perhaps if I could --

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG
utterances.text: It was promulgated in the Official Gazette of the 9th of December, but I think that it came into effect on the date it was made, it was issued.

utterances.speaker: MS. LAMB
utterances.text: Mrs. Alajbeg --

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG
utterances.text: Or rather --

utterances.speaker: MS. LAMB
utterances.text: -- Rephrase my question. Within this document itself, from what point --

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Objection, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Petrovic -- could I ask you to wait, please, a moment. Yes, Mr. Petrovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I object. The witness answered the question very clearly. The witness stated that this conclusion came into effect on the date it was issued. I don't see why my learned friend continues to insist and why she is about to put the same question again, after receiving a reply. Of course, the witness can clarify, but the question was put and the answer was given.

utterances.speaker: MS. LAMB
utterances.text: Perhaps I could --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I may --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: If you would wait a moment please, Ms. Lamb. You're quite right, Mr. Petrovic. We've noted the question and we've noted the answer. I believe Ms. Lamb is now to rephrase and put another question, but that doesn't overcome the fact that there has already been an answer given, and we've noted that. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Now, Ms. Lamb.

utterances.speaker: MS. LAMB
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: And could I mention that I've noticed a couple of times you have moved on to another question whilst the interpretation is still continuing to the witness. It requires a little bit of patience until the interpretation is finished before you move to your next question. We applaud your desire to get on quickly, but I think it would only confuse the witness to try and listen to two people at once.

utterances.speaker: MS. LAMB
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I'm much obliged.

utterances.speaker: MS. LAMB
utterances.text: Mrs. Alajbeg, could you kindly read the first sentence which immediately follows the word "conclusion" within this document.

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG
utterances.text: I have to go back to this conclusion. I think that it is so clear in itself, it speaks for itself. Because the conclusion pertains to the date when the function of Stjepan Mesic is terminated. The conclusion itself states that this date is the 8th of October. I only said that the conclusion was made on the 5th of December, but its effect is as of the 8th of October, because that is the date when all public law connections were broken. So whatever anyone did on behalf of the Republic of Croatia after that date would have no effect. We cannot speculate about when his function ceased, because the conclusion says it was on the 8th of October. There may have been a misunderstanding, because the conclusion was issued on the 5th of December but the effective date is 8th of October.

utterances.speaker: MS. LAMB
utterances.text: Thank you, Mrs. Alajbeg. May we now proceed to the documents contained at tab 9 within the Prosecution binder. Mrs. Alajbeg, do you recognise these documents, and if so, what are they collectively referred to as?

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG
utterances.text: Yes, I do recognise them. This is a set of opinions of the arbitration commission, popularly referred to as the Badinter Commission.

utterances.speaker: MS. LAMB
utterances.text: Can you describe briefly what the Badinter Commission was?

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG
utterances.text: The Badinter Commission was a body of the then-European Community, which tried to solve the crisis in the former Yugoslavia and established a conference on Yugoslavia, and within the scope of this conference, the Arbitration Committee was set up to give answers to the legal issues and the issues of contention between the sides.

utterances.speaker: MS. LAMB
utterances.text: Mrs. Alajbeg, could you kindly read the paragraph of the Badinter Commission's opinion number 1 of 29 November 1991, which is contained at the page bearing the ERN number 01171655. I apologise. That's 1656. In particular, I refer you now to paragraph 2A. Can you simply read out the conclusions contained in the first clause of this paragraph.

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG
utterances.text: The text is in English, so I will read it out in English. [In English] "The Arbitration Committee notes that although the SFRY has until now retained its international personality, notably inside international organisations, the Republics have expressed their desire for independence."

utterances.speaker: MS. LAMB
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you now turn to the following page, at paragraph 3. And again, could you read out the first conclusion of the arbitration committee.

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG
utterances.text: Number 3. In paragraph 3, the first conclusion is [In English] "Arbitration Committee is of the opinion that the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia is in the process of dissolution."

utterances.speaker: MS. LAMB
utterances.text: I would like to refer you to the conclusions of a later opinion of the same commission, opinion number 8, which is dated the 4th of July, 1993. It is found further on in the same -- tab of documents, at ERN number 00359855.

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG
utterances.text: Please excuse me. Could you tell me again the number of the opinion?

utterances.speaker: MS. LAMB
utterances.text: Yes. It's opinion number 8, and the specific page to which I would like you to refer is the page bearing ERN number 00359855. In particular, I would refer you to paragraph --

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG
utterances.text: Yes, I've found it.

utterances.speaker: MS. LAMB
utterances.text: -- paragraph 4, the final paragraph of that opinion, and ask you to read that out, please.

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG
utterances.text: Paragraph 4. [In English] "The Arbitration Commission is therefore of the opinion that the process of dissolution of the SFRY referred to in Opinion 1 of 29th of November, 1991, is now complete, and that the SFRY no longer exists."

utterances.speaker: MS. LAMB
utterances.text: Thank you. And finally, can I refer you to the last of the Badinter Commissions, number 11, which was rendered on the 16th of July, 1993, and which you will find as the last -- which you will -- which is the last document under tab 9. And I refer you in particular to the third and final page of that opinion, bearing ERN number 00359858.

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. LAMB
utterances.text: When does the Arbitration Commission therein determine the effective date of Croatian independence to have been?

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG
utterances.text: In paragraph 10 [In English] "... takes the view that the dates upon which the states stemming from the SFRY succeeded the SFRY, 8th October 1991, in the case of Republic of Croatia and the Republic of Slovenia.

utterances.speaker: MS. LAMB
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Mrs. Alajbeg, just to give you an indication of where we are in this testimony, we have now concluded the first section that I referred to at the outset, and I am now going to consider the recognition of Croatia by other states during this period. I would refer you at this point to the document contained at tab 10 of the Prosecution binder. Mrs. Alajbeg, do you recognise this document, and if so, could you briefly describe it.

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG
utterances.text: This document is issued by the Ministry of Foreign Affairs, and it's found on our website. It gives the dates of recognition and the dates of establishing diplomatic relations with other countries in alphabetical order.

utterances.speaker: MS. LAMB
utterances.text: Mrs. Alajbeg, could I now refer you to the documents contained at tab 11. The various documents at tab 11, Mrs. Alajbeg, can you describe briefly, in general terms, what they are?

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG
utterances.text: These documents in tab 11 are documents on the recognition of the Republic of Croatia, not all of them, of course, just some examples of such documents, from which it is evident how Croatia came to be recognised in the international community. These are relatively early documents of recognition.

utterances.speaker: MS. LAMB
utterances.text: Mrs. Alajbeg, from a survey both of these individual statements of recognition to which you have referred and the list showing the overall pattern with regard to recognition, could you comment briefly, could you briefly describe to the Court, the dates upon which the earliest recognitions of the state of Croatia occurred, just approximately.

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG
utterances.text: The first recognitions of the Republic of Croatia began on the date of its declaration of independence, that is, on the 25th of June, when Croatia and Slovenia recognised each other. Then we have the 30th of July, when we see that Latvia recognised Croatia. Then we have recognition by other Baltic states, up until December. I'm trying to find the document now. This is the Lithuanian one, but I know that we have documents from other Baltic states in the same year. Then we have recognition by Ukraine. I know that the Vatican recognised Croatia on the 12th of December, 1991. And finally, on the 13th of January, then we have -- just a moment, because there are also translations here. We have Latvia, on the 14th of December, 1991; Estonia, on the 13th of January, 1992; San Marino, on the 14th of January. These are all countries that recognised Croatia before the European Community as a whole recognised Croatia. We have the Ukraine, on the 11th of December; Iceland, before that date. I'm trying to find Iceland. It was certainly before the 15th of January, 1992, when all the countries of the European Community, as it was then, recognised Croatia. These are just some examples of recognition.

utterances.speaker: MS. LAMB
utterances.text: Thank you, Mrs. Alajbeg. Could I ask you to clarify for the record the date on which Latvia recognised the state of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG
utterances.text: The 14th of December, 1991.

utterances.speaker: MS. LAMB
utterances.text: And what about Lithuania?

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG
utterances.text: Just let me find it. The 30th of July, 1991.

utterances.speaker: MS. LAMB
utterances.text: Thank you. Mrs. Alajbeg, from your survey of the totality of the recognition statements in front of you and the list in front of you, when would you say that momentum with regard to Croatian recognition started to build, and when would it be fair to say that most states recognised the state of Croatia?

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG
utterances.text: With respect to Europe and a good part of other countries in the world, the process started on the 15th of January, 1992, when all the countries of the European Community recognised Croatia. There were instances of recognition both before and after that date, but the general recognition is viewed as having taken place when Croatia joined the United Nations, and this happened in April 1992.

utterances.speaker: MS. LAMB
utterances.text: Thank you. Did your duties as head of the international law section of the Croatian Ministry of Foreign Affairs include advising your foreign minister on whether or not to accord recognition to particular states? This question isn't asked in reference to any document at this point. Perhaps if I may clarify my question. In general terms, did your duties as a legal advisor to the foreign ministry extend to giving advice on issues of recognition?

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG
utterances.text: All the documents on recognition arrived in our department, because we had a collection of international treaties and intersection documents. Not only this, but every document, for the purpose of responding to it, passed through our department. As for the acts of recognition themselves, each act of recognition at that time was extremely welcome. So we didn't have to give advice on whether to accept this or not, because we accepted all these documents and recognition. But as for other states, we were happy to recognise them if they met all the requirements for their own sovereignty. But of course it was more others who recognised us than we them, because we were a newly created state.

utterances.speaker: MS. LAMB
utterances.text: Let's follow on from this, Mrs. Alajbeg. In providing advice on according recognition to others, even acknowledging that you were infrequently called upon to do so, what types of advice would you seek to provide in such a situation to your foreign minister? What would you aim to avoid in giving such advice, or to ensure in giving such advice?

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG
utterances.text: We endeavoured, with respect to our legal infrastructure, to solve issues as quickly as possible. One such issue was establishing diplomatic relations, because Croatia wanted to become an international legal personality as soon as possible and enter into diplomatic relations with others. So that we would immediately establish diplomatic relations after recognition, in order to raise our relations to a higher level, and this would include an act of recognition.

utterances.speaker: MS. LAMB
utterances.text: In according recognition to a state or advising that such recognition ought to be given, would such advice be given casually or lightly?

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG
utterances.text: If a country met the requirements, we advised that that state be recognised. That's how we accorded recognition to other states that arose on the territory of other composite states, on the territory of Czechoslovakia, the former Soviet Union, for example. But we did not accord recognition to the Republic of Northern Cyprus, the Turkish Republic of Northern Cyprus, which did recognise Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MS. LAMB
utterances.text: Why not?

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG
utterances.text: Because that state did not meet the requirement for international legal recognition, and it is not an international legal entity today.

utterances.speaker: MS. LAMB
utterances.text: What particular requirements did this entity not meet, in the view of your government?

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG
utterances.text: I just want to go back and establish that according to international legal theory, the prevailing theory, the act of recognition is not a constituent but a declaratory act. A state is -- what I want to say is that recognition is a factual and not a legal act. This is the prevailing theory today. Therefore, if a state meets the fundamental requirements, that is, it has its own territory, its population, and its organised government, and it desires to function as an international legal entity, then that state is an international legal entity. Recognition only confirms this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I wonder, Ms. Lamb, whether that's a convenient moment.

utterances.speaker: MS. LAMB
utterances.text: It would indeed be a convenient moment to break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: You've had an hour and a half there, Ms. Alajbeg, and I think it would be convenient for us now to have a morning break. The break will be for 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Ms. Lamb.

utterances.speaker: MS. LAMB
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. LAMB
utterances.text: Mrs. Alajbeg, before the break, we had more or less concluded our consideration of issues of recognition. There is, however, just one matter I would like to canvass before we head on to the next point and that is the issue of national minorities within Croatia. Is Croatia entirely ethnically and nationally homogeneous? And I'm not at this point referring to any document.

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG
utterances.text: Croatia has over 90 per cent of its populations who are Croats. However, there are other ethnic groups in Croatia. Most of the minorities in Croatia are Serbs. There are also Italians, Hungarians, Czechs, Slovaks. There are Albanians, and other ethnic groups.

utterances.speaker: MS. LAMB
utterances.text: We have already canvassed the EU response to the break-up of the former Yugoslavia generally. I would like now to turn to the position taken by the Badinter Commission on the particular question of national minorities. And in this regard, could you please refer to the fifth opinion of the Badinter Commission, which is contained at tab 9 of the document binder, at ERN number 02989714. It is opinion number 5, which is the third document within that bundle. And I would refer you in particular to the second page of that document, at paragraph 3. Could you perhaps indicate when you have found that paragraph.

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG
utterances.text: Yes, I've found it.

utterances.speaker: MS. LAMB
utterances.text: Within paragraph 3, what conclusions does the Arbitration Commission draw about the adequacy of the protections accorded to national minorities by Croatia?

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG
utterances.text: This opinion refers to the request by the Republic of Croatia for recognition. The opinion describes what Croatia has done with this regard. However, the last paragraph states that: [In English] "The constitutional act of 4 December 1991 does not fully incorporate all the provisions of the draft Convention of the 4th November 1991, notably, those contained in Chapter II, Article 2(c), under the heading special status." [Interpretation] Item 2 of that same paragraph says the following: [In English] "The authorities of the Republic of Croatia should therefore supplement the Constitutional Act in such a way as to satisfy those provisions."

utterances.speaker: MS. LAMB
utterances.text: So it would therefore seem, Mrs. Alajbeg, that the Arbitration Commission was not entirely satisfied with all details on this matter at this point. But can you nevertheless proceed to the third subclause of this paragraph and their conclusions with regard to the necessary conditions for recognition.

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG
utterances.text: "Subject to this reservation, the Republic of Croatia meets the necessary conditions for its recognition by the Member States of the European Community in accordance with the Declaration on Yugoslavia and the Guidelines on the Recognition of New States in Eastern Europe and in the Soviet Union, adopted by the Council of the European Communities on 16 December 1991."

utterances.speaker: MS. LAMB
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Mrs. Alajbeg, I'm going to now leave the Badinter Commission findings, and I'm going to refer you back to your time as the chief international lawyer for the Croatian foreign ministry. During this period, did you ever advise your foreign minister to withhold recognition from a state purely because of unresolved domestic minority rights issues that may have existed within that country?

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: MS. LAMB
utterances.text: Thank you. In a similar vein, did you ever advise your foreign minister to withhold recognition from a state purely because its borders may have been contested or because it was suffering from high levels of internal strife?

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG
utterances.text: The answer is no as well.

utterances.speaker: MS. LAMB
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, that concludes this portion of my direct examination pertaining to recognition practice. I'm now going to turn to the third element that I wish to examine, and that, in general, refers to the effectiveness of Croatian state organs within this period. I would ask at this point that you refer to the documents contained, the official documents which are contained at tab 12 of the binder. Mrs. Alajbeg, you will see that there are many -- that this tab is extremely lengthy, and there are many instruments contained therein. But in general terms, what are these documents?

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG
utterances.text: I believe that this is a series of documents passed by the parliament of the Republic of Croatia or some other organs, and these documents constitute a number of laws and by-laws and decisions which are all necessary for the proper functioning of a state.

utterances.speaker: MS. LAMB
utterances.text: And are all of these documents contained in the Official Gazette of the Republic of Croatia?

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG
utterances.text: Yes. For the most part, although it is not mandatory for all the by-laws to be published in the Official Gazette.

utterances.speaker: MS. LAMB
utterances.text: Okay. I will refer to each of these instruments in turn now. Could you now go, please, to the first page of this document bundle, dated -- which is the Croatian Official Gazette dated 4th of November, 1991, bearing the ERN number 00894321.

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. LAMB
utterances.text: In particular, I would refer you to the index that you see on that page, and could you tell me the subject areas to which the following document numbers refer: 1552, 1557, and 1558. Could you please take each one by one.

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG
utterances.text: The first one is the decree on ranks, assignment of ranks, promotion into a higher rank, and uniforms of members of the armed forces of the Republic of Croatia. This is not a law; this is a by-law, actually, it's a decree, which deals with the issues of ranks and rank accorded to the members of the armed forces.

utterances.speaker: MS. LAMB
utterances.text: And the next document, document number 1557, to what does that refer?

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG
utterances.text: This is a very interesting document. This is the ratification of the agreement on payment transactions between the Republic of Croatia and the Republic of Slovenia. So this is an international agreement which was signed by the two internationally recognised subjects, which had recognised each other as well. And the government ratifies this agreement on payment and transactions, and this agreement then becomes an international agreement.

utterances.speaker: MS. LAMB
utterances.text: Mrs. Alajbeg, before we look at document 1557 in more detail, can you merely read the title of the following document, document 1558.

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG
utterances.text: Yes. This is the book of rules on military booklet, or military ID.

utterances.speaker: MS. LAMB
utterances.text: Thank you. Let us now return to the document that you previously mentioned, namely, number 1557. Now, the text of that instrument is contained at ERN number 00894332, and I would ask that you proceed to that page now.

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG
utterances.text: Yes, I've found it.

utterances.speaker: MS. LAMB
utterances.text: Again, could you refer -- could you tell us today what generally this instrument is.

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG
utterances.text: This is an agreement on payment transactions between two states: The Republic of Slovenia and the Republic of Croatia. This international agreement was published in both languages, in Slovenian and in Croatian, and the government hereby ratifies this international agreement. This agreement regulates the terms of payment between the two republics; the currency is mentioned here, as well as the ways the whole payment transaction should be carried out between the two states. The document clearly shows that both states act as independent international subjects and enter an international agreement to deal with that part of their mutual relations. The wording follows the rules of the wording of an international agreement. It contains all of the necessary clauses which define such an international legal enactment.

utterances.speaker: MS. LAMB
utterances.text: Mrs. Alajbeg, what date -- at what date did this international agreement come into effect? And if possible, at what date was it negotiated, if that is clear from the text?

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG
utterances.text: Just a moment, please. Article 7 of this agreement says that this agreement shall come into effect on the day when both parties inform each other that the procedure had been carried out in keeping with the national legislation of each of the republics. This is the wording used in international agreements. And it will come into effect on the 8th of October, 1991, which is the date when both states, according to the Badinter's Commission, became international subjects. And as of that date, they became legal subjects. The date is the date of succession.

utterances.speaker: MS. LAMB
utterances.text: This instrument itself, in its concluding paragraph, contains what date?

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG
utterances.text: In Zagreb and in Ljubljana, on the 29th of October. However, it became effective as of the 8th of October.

utterances.speaker: MS. LAMB
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I would now like to proceed through this same exhibit bundle to the second document. I'm referring at this point to the Croatian Official Gazette of the 4th of December, 1991, the index to which is found at the page bearing the ERN number 00328714.

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG
utterances.text: The following document -- just a moment, please. 714, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. LAMB
utterances.text: Have you found the page to which I refer?

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG
utterances.text: I have.

utterances.speaker: MS. LAMB
utterances.text: Could you please briefly describe the type and the subject matter of the documents bearing the following numbers: 1663 -- I will allow you to speak to that title first.

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG
utterances.text: This is the decision on the proclamation of the constitutional law on human rights and freedoms and on the rights of ethnic and national communities or minorities in the Republic of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MS. LAMB
utterances.text: Now, document number 1665?

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG
utterances.text: 1665 is the decision on the establishment of a foreign office of the Republic of Croatia in Ottawa, Canada.

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG
utterances.text: This is a decree on promoting officers into active officers.

utterances.speaker: MS. LAMB
utterances.text: That would be within the Croatian army?

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG
utterances.text: [In English] Within Croatian army, yes. [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. LAMB
utterances.text: And finally, document number 1770.

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG
utterances.text: 1770 -- I apologise. Are you referring to the same Official Gazette here? 1670, I believe.

utterances.speaker: MS. LAMB
utterances.text: I apologise. You are correct. 1670.

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG
utterances.text: This is a decree on assigning ranks and promoting officers into higher ranks.

utterances.speaker: MS. LAMB
utterances.text: Again, within the Croatian army?

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: MS. LAMB
utterances.text: Finally, I would like to proceed to the third and the final document within this bundle. I am referring here to the Croatian Official Gazette of the 8th of October, 1991, whose first page, the index page, bears the ERN number 00894265.

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. LAMB
utterances.text: Mrs. Alajbeg, could you please describe the types of instruments which are listed down the left-hand column of this index, and what remarks, if any, would you make about the significance of their subject matter?

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG
utterances.text: On the 8th of October, 1991, when the important decision was passed on dissolving relations between the republics, the parliament of Croatia passed a number of decrees, by-laws, laws, decisions, as well as a number of laws on adopting formal federal laws in their parts. This was done in order for the Republic of Croatia to regulate its legal infrastructure and for it to be able to function normally. Because as of that date, all the formerly existing legal ties with the former state stopped existing. Regardless of the fact that Croatia, throughout 1991, from the time when the constitution was passed in 1990, throughout 1991, the legislative activity was very busy. There was a very busy time around the date of the declaration of independence in June 1991. However, the whole procedure had to be completed before the 8th of October. On that date, Croatia became an international legal subject and had all the functions like any other state. For that reason, in this Official Gazette - and I believe that several issues were published on the same date - you'll find a number of legal acts, laws and by-laws which regulated different spheres of life.

utterances.speaker: MS. LAMB
utterances.text: Could you elaborate on what some of these difference spheres are?

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG
utterances.text: For example, I can read some titles.

utterances.speaker: MS. LAMB
utterances.text: That would be very helpful. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG
utterances.text: For example, there is a decision on ratifying the decree on the recognition of the Republic of Estonia. This is just one example. So Estonia and Lithuania, which were recognised at the same time, and there is the law on Croatian citizenship, the law on residence and temporary residence of citizens; the law on travel documents held by Croatian citizens; the law on personal identity card; the law on foreign affairs; the law on entering and implementing international agreements; then the law on public accountancy system; the law on customs; the law on market inspection --

utterances.speaker: MS. LAMB
utterances.text: Mrs. Alajbeg --

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG
utterances.text: -- and similar laws.

utterances.speaker: MS. LAMB
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Within the list you have just provided, I would like now to refer your attention particularly to two of these instruments, numbered 1276 and 1277. Before we begin, can you reiterate what is the subject matter of these two documents.

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG
utterances.text: These two documents deal with foreign affairs and entering in and implementing international agreements and contracts.

utterances.speaker: MS. LAMB
utterances.text: Now, what involvement did you personally have within the preparation of these two instruments?

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG
utterances.text: My role was to draft these documents. Since I was among the rare persons who had worked in the former federal foreign ministry. We prepared these drafts, since none of us had any other experience, by compromising between the former federal law on foreign affairs and the law on entering in and implementing international agreements, and the constitution that was then in effect. Every law had to be in accordance with the constitution. So we had to adjust the law to the constitution, because the role of the former parliament in the former state differed from the role of the parliament in Croatia, because president had some of the roles that the parliament had in the former state.

utterances.speaker: MS. LAMB
utterances.text: You have just mentioned, and indeed you have previously mentioned also, that the Croatian assembly during this period frequently incorporated certain laws of the SFRY within Croatia. As somebody who was closely involved in this process, can you explain why this approach was so frequently taken?

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG
utterances.text: I would say that that was a procedure that made part of internal succession. The whole legislative infrastructure that existed in the former SFRY, irrespective of whether this was a federal legislation or a republican legislation, dealt with a number of issues in great detail, so we did not have any reason not to adopt some of those solutions which conformed with our system. We wanted to make things as simple as possible when dealing with this problem. That is why the Croatian parliament incorporated in their entirety or most of the legal text as their own laws, until the moment entirely new regulations were to be passed. This bought us some time when it came to dealing with Croatian legislation. The same thing applied to the international sphere. Based on the succession, we adopted international agreements that had been entered into by the former state. The foundation for that was a decision passed on the 8th of October, as well as the declaration which was passed on the 25th of June, 1991. Both of these documents said that Republic of Croatia would continue to honour all of its international obligations that arose from the international agreements entered into by the former state if those obligations applied to the Republic of Croatia and if they were not contrary to the constitution and the legal system of the Republic of Croatia. In that way, we could adopt most of the former agreements, and there were about 3.000 of them. We incorporated those into our system. When it came to bilateral agreements, we entered into those with particular states, and those were agreements on the succession of particular former agreements.

utterances.speaker: MS. LAMB
utterances.text: Mrs. Alajbeg, I apologise for interrupting. The -- we will indeed return to the issue of succession to treaty obligations at a later point. I wonder, however, at this juncture, if I could return to domestic Croatian legal instruments for one moment longer. Many of the instruments which have been admitted today seem to be decrees, or else quite sparse in their content. Again, on the basis of your involvement in the process at the time, could you elaborate as to why much of the early Croatian legislation often took this form? That is, why was there --

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG
utterances.text: Are you referring to decrees?

utterances.speaker: MS. LAMB
utterances.text: Yes. Both decrees and also very brief pieces of legislation which appears to be scant elaboration. Are there any reasons for why this may have been the case?

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG
utterances.text: Like in every other state, under extraordinary circumstances, decrees were passed with legal effect. Those decrees would later on be ratified by the parliament. The situation at the time was not normal, and the parliament sometimes could not sit physically.

utterances.speaker: MS. LAMB
utterances.text: Mrs. Alajbeg, you've perhaps quite euphemistically referred to the circumstances of the time being not normal. In fact, the armed conflict was still ongoing in this period; is this correct?

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG
utterances.text: Yes. These extraordinary circumstances don't necessarily have to be an armed conflict. However, in Croatia, the situation was extraordinary. I wouldn't agree with you that there were so many decrees; the legislative activity was carried out in a normal way. If you look at all these documents, there are more proper legal documents. And as for the decrees which would then be ratified, I believe that there were fewer of those than the proper legal texts.

utterances.speaker: MS. LAMB
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I would refer you now to tab number 13 of our binder. Again, we see there are many instruments within this binder, but I would be obliged if you could comment, in general terms, on what these instruments are and where in particular they are published.

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG
utterances.text: This is document 265. I apologise. We are looking at two different binders.

utterances.speaker: MS. LAMB
utterances.text: I'm referring at this point to tab number 13. Could you confirm, these are official documents published where?

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG
utterances.text: They were published in the Official Gazette, number 4, on the 2nd of February, 1991.

utterances.speaker: MS. LAMB
utterances.text: That is indeed the first of the documents to which I will refer you now, and this document -- in particular, within this document, I will refer to that containing the number 86. What is the subject matter of this document?

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG
utterances.text: This is the law on general defence, the expunged version, which shows that there was the original version and some amendments, and that the expunged version was actually published in the Official Gazette. And the document's title is "The law on general defence."

utterances.speaker: MS. LAMB
utterances.text: Now, this document -- was this document a federal document or a republican law or a federal law, and what date does it bear?

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG
utterances.text: This is a republican law. This is not a federal defence law. This is the republican defence law. At that time, the republics as well had their respective defence laws, because they had some authorities within the scope of defence, particularly in the field of Territorial Defence.

utterances.speaker: MS. LAMB
utterances.text: I would now like you, Mrs. Alajbeg, to move to the second document within this bundle, which is published in the Croatian Official Gazette, bearing the ERN number 00894235. It is some way through the documents under this bundle, approximately one half to two-thirds of the way though the totality of the documents.

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG
utterances.text: This new issue -- different issue of the Official Gazette? I'm looking at the issue number.

utterances.speaker: MS. LAMB
utterances.text: The version I am looking for -- yes, in particular, number 49. Can you indicate when you have found the first page of that document. If it would assist, I can reread the ERN number and question. Are you now at ERN number --

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG
utterances.text: 4235. What is the ERN number, please? 4235. This is the law on defence, which was published in the Official Gazette issue number 49, dated 20 September 1991.

utterances.speaker: MS. LAMB
utterances.text: Thank you. And within that document, within that gazette, can I refer you to document number 1230. What is the title of that document? Again, it commences on the first page.

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG
utterances.text: Yes. Decree promulgating the law on defence. And the law itself is called the law on defence.

utterances.speaker: MS. LAMB
utterances.text: And when did this law come into effect?

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG
utterances.text: I have to see, because evidently the decree was dated the 28th of June, 1991. The law was published on the 20th of September, 1991, but we have to see the final provisions in order to see when the law took effect. This law shall come into effect on the date of its publication in the Official Gazette. If the date of publication is the 20th of September, 1991, then that is the date when this law took effect.

utterances.speaker: MS. LAMB
utterances.text: What is the difference between this law and the law on defence, to which we have previously referred?

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG
utterances.text: The law we spoke about before was passed in the '80s, and then the revised version was published in February 1991. The difference between these two laws is that now Croatia has its own law on defence and is no longer applying the federal law on defence.
