The former law was the republican law, which was an addendum to the federal law and applied only to the territory of the Republic of Croatia and dealt with the authorities of the local communities in the area of defence, whereas the new law has provisions covering all areas, the rights and duties of all citizens of the Republic of Croatia, the administrative bodies, the defence of the territorial integrity, and the constitutional order of the Republic of Croatia. It deals with the armed forces of the Republic of Croatia, compulsory military service, and other issues of significance for the defence system. So this is an independent law of the Republic of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MS. LAMB
utterances.text: Mrs. Alajbeg, I'm going to now refer you to the final instrument within this bundle, and that is toward the end of these documents and bears the first page number 00894295. I refer -- can you kindly confirm for the record the type and nature of the document that you are now looking at.

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG
utterances.text: In the Official Gazette number 53A of the 8th of October, 1991, if this is the document in question --

utterances.speaker: MS. LAMB
utterances.text: And within the index --

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG
utterances.text: -- the number 1350 is the law on amendments to the law of defence. This is the law on defence that we mentioned before, and now it is being amended, because this is the law on amendments to the law on defence. The legislative activity in the field of defence was very active, as we can see.

utterances.speaker: MS. LAMB
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I'm now going to refer you to tab number 14 within the document binder. Again for the record, can you describe the first page of the document before you, ERN number 00894260.

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG
utterances.text: Yes. On page 1 again, we have a list of laws and by-laws. The Official Gazette is dated the 3rd of October, 1991, and this is issue number 52. For example, under number 1244, we have an example of the taking over of certain laws from the field of defence, former federal laws which are now applied in the Republic of Croatia as republican regulations.

utterances.speaker: MS. LAMB
utterances.text: And what about document 1247?

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG
utterances.text: This is a decree on the taking over of assets of the JNA and the SSNO, which was the federal secretariat for National Defence, on the territory of the Republic of Croatia, which were owned by the Republic of Croatia. So there was a decree that these assets would be taken over and would become the ownership of the Republic of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MS. LAMB
utterances.text: The process that you have just referred to in these two documents, is this common to the process you have described in relation to many of the other instruments that have been admitted as legislative instruments of Croatia?

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG
utterances.text: You mean other areas of activity?

utterances.speaker: MS. LAMB
utterances.text: Not really their subject matter; the process that you describe of laws being adopted and taking over, does this -- is this another example similar to the ones you gave previously on this matter?

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG
utterances.text: Correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. LAMB
utterances.text: Thank you. I will now turn you to tab number 15. Could you state what type of document it is and its date, please.

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG
utterances.text: Again, it's an Official Gazette, number 73, of the 31st of December, 1991.

utterances.speaker: MS. LAMB
utterances.text: Thank you. I'm going to stay with the first index page of this Official Gazette and refer you in particular to the titles of a number of documents. These document numbers are 1864 through to 1878. Can you comment on what the Croatian assembly sought to achieve via these decrees?

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG
utterances.text: The first two documents are conclusions, and the next series of documents are decisions on the recognition of the former Soviet republics as independent states.

utterances.speaker: MS. LAMB
utterances.text: On what date did Croatia recognise these states?

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG
utterances.text: Evidently, this was published in the Official Gazette. We will just look at the date now. The dates are the 28th of December. This was the recognition at the session of the parliament on the 28th of December, 1991 --

utterances.speaker: MS. LAMB
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG
utterances.text: -- for all the former Soviet republics.

utterances.speaker: MS. LAMB
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, finally on this issue, Mrs. Alajbeg, would you say that all of the legislative instruments we have been discussing this morning, and the other official documents that we have referred, would these represent all of those produced by the Croatian state organs during late 1991?

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. LAMB
utterances.text: There would be, in your view, no other legislative instruments passed during this period?

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG
utterances.text: There was a whole series of legal instruments that were passed by various ministries and bodies of government administration, but these were not necessarily published in the Official Gazette. They would be published in the gazettes of these bodies. So the activity was far greater. These were various technical regulations, by-laws, and so on and so forth. All this was part of enormous legislative activity taking place in Croatia at the time.

utterances.speaker: MS. LAMB
utterances.text: So if I understand your testimony correctly, the documents that we have mentioned today in fact are simply a small sample of the totality of instruments that one could find if one looked; would that be correct?

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG
utterances.text: Yes, correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. LAMB
utterances.text: Mrs. Alajbeg, what similarities, if any, could you observe between the state structures that were in place at this time in Croatia and those of the present-day Republic of Croatia, in terms of both their structure and function, if that would assist?

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG
utterances.text: There is continuity. We still have the constitution of 1990, and many of these laws that we have just mentioned. Therefore, we are functioning or have been functioning as a state since then.

utterances.speaker: MS. LAMB
utterances.text: Thank you. And overall, Mrs. Alajbeg, what observations did you make regarding the efficacy of the Croatian state organs during this period? How comprehensive was its legislative activity around this time?

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG
utterances.text: In spite of understaffing at all levels, Croatia simply had to consolidate, and there was an enormous amount of activity. As a civil servant in one of these bodies, all I can say is there were no office hours. We worked under all kinds of circumstances. When Zagreb was bombed, the parliament had its session in the INA company in the basement. They sat there in the basement for days on end, passing laws.

utterances.speaker: MS. LAMB
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Mrs. Alajbeg, that concludes, actually, the third portion of my examination-in-chief on this issue.

utterances.speaker: MS. LAMB
utterances.text: Your Honours, if it would be convenient, this would be an ideal time for a break. I'm equally happy to move on to the next point, if required.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I think it preferable that you continue. Our timing is directed not only to our personal convenience, but the needs of those who are assisting us outside the courtroom, and it would be better if we continued for a little time.

utterances.speaker: MS. LAMB
utterances.text: Very well, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. LAMB
utterances.text: Mrs. Alajbeg, we've referred to, in great detail, many documents that were produced more or less contemporaneously with the conflict in Croatia. I'm now going to be moving to the final category of issues to be addressed here, and these are instead documents which were produced subsequent to the conflict, and other forms of practice which is noticeable only at a later date. I would ask you at this point to return to binder number 9 - sorry - to tab number 9, the Badinter Commission findings to which we have referred earlier. Would you please indicate when you have found Opinion number 11 of the Badinter Commission, bearing ERN number 00359856.

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG
utterances.text: Yes, I have found the document.

utterances.speaker: MS. LAMB
utterances.text: I would refer you in particular to its final paragraph, found on ERN number -- page number 00359858.

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG
utterances.text: This is Opinion number 11; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MS. LAMB
utterances.text: That is correct. Again, I'm referring you in particular to paragraph 10. Could you kindly indicate when you have found this paragraph.

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG
utterances.text: Yes, I've found it.

utterances.speaker: MS. LAMB
utterances.text: And could you simply recap for the Court the date upon which the Badinter Commission found Croatia to have seceded from the SFRY.

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG
utterances.text: The date of succession was the date from which Croatia is definitely considered an independent legal entity in the international community, the date on which it took over all its rights and obligations, as confirmed by a series of documents in the international community. I would especially like to mention depositories of the secretary-general of the UN. I think there are examples here in the material of various countries recognising that the 8th of October is the date in question.

utterances.speaker: MS. LAMB
utterances.text: Mrs. Alajbeg, we will indeed get to those documents in just a couple of moments. But before we leave paragraph 10 of the Badinter Commission, could you simply indicate the date upon which the Badinter Commission made its ultimate conclusions on the basis of all evidence before it. The date is found on the bottom of Opinion number 11.

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG
utterances.text: The date is the 16th of July, 1993. That is the date of this opinion.

utterances.speaker: MS. LAMB
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG
utterances.text: However --

utterances.speaker: MS. LAMB
utterances.text: Thank you very much. At this point, Mrs. Alajbeg, I will ask you to move to binder -- tab number 16 within the binder. Are you now at that place in the binder?

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG
utterances.text: Yes, I have.

utterances.speaker: MS. LAMB
utterances.text: I refer you to the document numbered on this particular document as number 196. But I wonder if you can identify that document, and if so, describe to the Court what it is.

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG
utterances.text: Document number 196 contains the General Assembly resolution number 46/238, on admission of Croatia to United Nations membership.

utterances.speaker: MS. LAMB
utterances.text: And this resolution --

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG
utterances.text: [In English] Adopted at the 86th plenary meeting, 22nd May, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MS. LAMB
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I would now at this point request the ushers to hand the text which I have here to both the witness, the Bench, and our learned friends. I am referring you now to Article 4 of the United Nations Charter. According to Article 4(1) of this text, to whom is membership of the United Nations open?

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG
utterances.text: [Interpretation] According to Article 4, paragraph 1, the following can become a member of the United Nations. I will read it out in English. [In English] "The membership in the United Nations is open to all other peace-loving states which accepts the obligations contained in the present charter and, in the judgement of the organisation, are able and willing to carry out these obligations."

utterances.speaker: MS. LAMB
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, Article 4(1) refers to all other states, presumably because Article 4(2) refers to the initial membership of the United Nations. Very briefly, who comprised the initial -- that initial membership? States of -- the original signatory states of this treaty?

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All other states, of course, which means any future member, any future state. So these are peace-loving states who accept the obligations mentioned in the charter. Of course, the decision of the organisation is necessary, and this decision was made at a session of the General Assembly.

utterances.speaker: MS. LAMB
utterances.text: At that point, Mrs. Alajbeg, I would like to perhaps interrupt, because the decision that would have been made in the General Assembly on the 22nd of May, 1992 would have been made on what basis, pursuant to what conclusion of the totality of the membership of the United Nations? This doesn't refer to the text of the document.

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG
utterances.text: Of course, the decision was made on the basis of a request by the Republic of Croatia. Every state has to apply, and Croatia did that. And along with the application, a letter was forwarded from the president of the republic, in which he explains the reasons why Croatia wishes to become a member of the UN and why it should become a member of the UN. The formal application is a conventional text in which Croatia agrees to accept the principles of the charter.

utterances.speaker: MS. LAMB
utterances.text: Mrs. Alajbeg, this resolution would nevertheless suggest that Croatia was not -- doesn't suggest, it states that Croatia was not normally admitted as a member until the 22nd of May, 1992. Would it follow from this that Croatia therefore did not meet all requirements of statehood immediately prior to that date?

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG
utterances.text: Certainly not. Not every state has to be a member of the United Nations. A state may not wish to be a member, or there may be reasons for the UN not to accept such a state. We know very well that such states do exist. We have also established that joining a certain organisation, or the recognition of a state, is not the constituent act for the creation of that state. Therefore, Croatia simply confirmed its desire to participate actively in the international community, and by receiving Croatia, the international community recognised that Croatia was a peace-loving country and that it wished to communicate with Croatia in all the ways provided for in the documents of that organisation.

utterances.speaker: MS. LAMB
utterances.text: If I understand you correctly, then, while you are saying that admittance of Croatia to membership on this date, although that would suggest that the UN membership was satisfied as to Croatian statehood, it is likely that Croatia had satisfied the necessary preconditions for membership at some date prior. Would that be an accurate summary of your testimony?

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG
utterances.text: We consider that we met these requirements, that is, Croatia considers that it met these requirements when it constituted itself as a state. That is, if not before, then definitely on the 25th of June, when it declared its independence, in 1991. Croatia is considered to be a state since that date, and it has acted as a state since then. The delay of three months until the 8th of October was agreed on, and because there was no improvement of the situation on the territory of the former Yugoslavia, Croatia, on the 8th of October, completely broke all state and legal relations. So we used this date, the 8th of October, in our official documents, although we can consider that the 25th of June is a very important act in the creation of Croatian statehood.

utterances.speaker: MS. LAMB
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you very much. I would like at this point to move to another issue, and that concerns membership of other international organisations. Around the end of 1991, did Croatia seek membership of international organisations other than the United Nations?

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG
utterances.text: Yes. After the 8th of October, the government was charged by the parliament to apply to various international organisations in order for Croatia to join these organisations. This was not only an act of recognition of Croatia; it was also a necessity for Croatia, because we had to communicate with a number of organisations, with a view to regulating life, starting from various technical organisations relating to traffic, trade, the protection of individual rights, the rights of individuals and various associations. So the activities began.

utterances.speaker: MS. LAMB
utterances.text: Thank you, Mrs. Alajbeg. I am at this point going to refer you right back, I'm afraid, to tab number 8 of the Prosecution Exhibit binder. Can you confirm for the record the type of document this is and its date and provenance, please.

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG
utterances.text: Official Gazette number 66, 9th December 1991.

utterances.speaker: MS. LAMB
utterances.text: Thank you. I'm going to refer you in particular on the index of this gazette to documents number 1678 through to 1680. Can you briefly describe the titles of these documents.

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG
utterances.text: The title of document 1678 is "Decision on applying to join the Council of Europe," and this is actually misstated as the European council in the Croatian version.

utterances.speaker: MS. LAMB
utterances.text: So if I understand you correctly, this indicates that Croatia sought admission to these bodies as of the 9th of December, 1991.

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG
utterances.text: This is an instruction issued by the parliament, which tasked the government on submitting a request.

utterances.speaker: MS. LAMB
utterances.text: The international organisations to which these instruments refer, are they examples of some of the organisations which Croatia sought membership of during this period? Were there others? I perhaps should rewind a little. Firstly, are these organisations those which Croatia sought membership to in this period?

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG
utterances.text: These are examples. These are the organisations that were important to Croatia at the time, the Council of Europe, the United Nations, the Central European Initiative. But not all the applications made by Croatia were published in the Official Gazettes. We didn't wait for the parliament to tell us to do this. We asked to join certain organisations pursuant to decisions made by the government. At the time, there was a lot of correspondence, a lot of contacts with various international organisations. For example, I remember personally contacting the International Standardisation Organisation, because we had to have car registration plates, we had to have the country abbreviation for these. We also contacted some organisations in connection with maritime activities. So there was a large number of organisations. I remember applying to the International Organisation for the Protection of Intellectual Copyright, and we joined that organisation on the 8th of October, 1991, and became a party to their basic documents.

utterances.speaker: MS. LAMB
utterances.text: Thank you very much. At this juncture, Mrs. Alajbeg, I'm going to turn to the very final area that I will canvass and this refers to the technical area of state succession to treaties.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I think, Ms. Lamb, that is a distinct topic. We've now reached a time where it would be convenient for us to have a break before launching into that. It will be a 20-minute break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Ms. Lamb.

utterances.speaker: MS. LAMB
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. LAMB
utterances.text: Mrs. Alajbeg, just prior to when we broke for a coffee break, you testified, and the transcript reference in question is on page 55, at lines 23 to 24. You were speaking at this point, and I would like to return to your testimony just to clarify one small matter. With regard -- you were speaking at this point with regards to organisations that Croatia deemed important to join, and you said at that point, and I quote: "But not all the applications made by Croatia were published in the Official Gazette. We didn't wait for the parliament to tell us to do this. We asked to join certain organisations pursuant to decisions made by the government." In this passage, you seem to distinguish between the words "government" and "parliament," and indeed in Croatian, I understand that the word for parliament is "sabor," while are government is "vlada". Can you explain very briefly for us what both these terms mean.

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG
utterances.text: Government is actually the cabinet, or the minister and the Prime Minister, and Sabor is our parliament. And that is the difference. However, when people talk about government, very often we refer to government per se, and what we mean is the main state structure. Very often, we refer to the president, to the Sabor, and the government. So when we say our government thinks this or that, then we take into account all the factors, which is not really very precise. However, in our case, the decision on these things, for example, when something -- when an organisation was very important, then it was the parliament to urge us to do as soon as possible. We did it routinely for all international organisations. I don't have a document in front of me; however, I remember that there were some instructions that told us to approach all the international organisations. It was a general decision that Croatia should, as soon as possible, become a member of all international organisations, to become an international subject as soon as possible, in all the possible ways.

utterances.speaker: MS. LAMB
utterances.text: Thank you very much. At this point, Mrs. Alajbeg, I will return to the final matter prefaced before the break, that being the matter of state succession to treaties. You testified previously that in the course of your career as a foreign ministry lawyer, you were once the head of the international treaty section of the federal ministry; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG
utterances.text: I apologise. I can't hear the interpreters very well. Can this be adjusted, the volume? It is much better now. I believe that I understood your question. Yes, I was in Germany from the beginning of 1991 to the moment I joined the Croatian Ministry of Foreign Affairs. I was the head of department for international treaties within the department for international legal affairs. In this department, I worked as an advisor. Now it's too loud. I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MS. LAMB
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG
utterances.text: I apologise. I believe it's too loud now. It's better now. Thank you. In that department, I worked even before I went abroad for my term of office there, so I'm familiar with --

utterances.speaker: MS. LAMB
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Would you say that you are, therefore, familiar with the legal regime governing treaties and the contemporary treaty practice of states, contemporary practice of states with regard to treaties in particular?

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MS. LAMB
utterances.text: Thank you. I will then refer you directly to tab number 18 within my -- within the Prosecution binder. There are two documents contained in this tab. Could you briefly tell the Court whether you recognise these instruments, and if so, what do you recognise them to be?

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG
utterances.text: Just a moment. I believe that this may be in a different binder.

utterances.speaker: MS. LAMB
utterances.text: I apologise, Mrs. Alajbeg. I withdraw this question. I meant to refer you instead to tab number 17, not tab number 18.

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG
utterances.text: [In English] 17, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. LAMB
utterances.text: Now, at tab number 17, there are numerous documents, but how collectively could these documents -- firstly, do you recognise what these documents are, and if so, what do you recognise them to be?

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I recognise these documents. These are depository notifications, number 1, number 2. Yes, these are depository notifications with regard to the succession of international treaties.

utterances.speaker: MS. LAMB
utterances.text: Thank you. And the individual -- the treaties to which these instruments refer are far too numerous to require listing before the Court today, but can you nevertheless describe the date upon which each of these instruments indicate as being the effective date of Croatian succession to these instruments?

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG
utterances.text: In a number of the depository notifications by the Secretary-General of the United Nations, he being the depository of the international treaties passed within the United Nations, one sentence is in common. [In English] "As of 8 October 1991, the date on which Croatia assumed responsibility for its international relations."

utterances.speaker: MS. LAMB
utterances.text: Thank you. And on what basis is that date indicated to be the effective date of succession?

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG
utterances.text: Again, I am not receiving the interpretation, I'm afraid.

utterances.speaker: MS. LAMB
utterances.text: Can you hear me now?

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG
utterances.text: I'm afraid I'm not receiving the interpretation loud and clear. Yes, now I can hear it. I didn't hear it before. It is a bit too loud, but I am receiving it now.

utterances.speaker: MS. LAMB
utterances.text: Having identified the 8th of October, 1991 as the date upon which the depository notifications declare these treaties to have been binding upon Croatia, I wonder if you can elaborate just slightly further and explain why this date was chosen as the effective date of succession. What is the basis for this date being selected, according to the text of any one of those instruments?

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG
utterances.text: The basis was obviously the widely accepted position by the international community that Croatia became an international subject and assumed its rights and responsibilities as such, as of the 8th October 1991 --

utterances.speaker: MS. LAMB
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG
utterances.text: -- which was confirmed later on by Badinter's Commission.

utterances.speaker: MS. LAMB
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I refer now to the final tab within the binder, namely, number 19. This tab contains two documents. Do you recognise these documents, and if so, what do you recognise them as being?

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG
utterances.text: I believe that this is document 717, 29891277. This is another -- this is a series of international treaties which are known as Geneva Conventions, and in more specifically, this is our request. However, behind that, there is also a depository notification. Croatia proposes to become party to Geneva instruments, the four conventions and the two protocols, as of a certain date, the day which has been established, and that is the date of succession. And the depository is the Swiss government, which in the following documents accepts that proposal. I can read this specific sentence. [In English] Republic of Croatia became a party to the conventions and the protocols as of the date of its independence on 8th October 1991."

utterances.speaker: MS. LAMB
utterances.text: Thank you. To be crystal clear for the sake of the record, let the record note that the witness has indicated that the date of effective Croatian succession to the Geneva Conventions and Protocols, in accordance with the depository notification contained in binder 18 is 8th of October, 1991.

utterances.speaker: MS. LAMB
utterances.text: Your Honours, that concludes my examination-in-chief. I have two further matters that I would like to raise, with your leave.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. LAMB
utterances.text: The first of these, Your Honours, refers to a correction that must be made to the transcript. I refer in this regard to page 34 of the transcript, at lines 7 to 10. Therein, the transcript records as follows: "Did you ever advise your foreign minister to withhold recognition from a state purely because its borders may have been contested or because it was suffering from high levels of international strife?" That last -- those last two words, "international strife," need to be stricken from the record and replaced with the words "internal strife.".

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Your observation is that the -- is it that it is suggested that you used the word "internal," but the record shows "international," or that you've now had a second thought as to what you should have said.

utterances.speaker: MS. LAMB
utterances.text: To the best of my recollection, Your Honour, it is the former, but I will stand corrected.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I must say, it accords with my recollection as well, but nevertheless, very well.

utterances.speaker: MS. LAMB
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I think we can arrange for that correction.

utterances.speaker: MS. LAMB
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. The final matter I'd like to bring your attention to -- to your attention is that I'm aware that in the course of my examination-in-chief today I have tendered an extremely large number of documents through this witness. I have therefore prepared a summary of the Prosecution evidence on this matter, which is not intended as a filing, but if it would be of assistance to the Bench in understanding the structure of the Prosecution case in this matter, I would be happy to put it at your disposal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I think it would assist us, and no doubt it would be of use to Defence counsel as well.

utterances.speaker: MS. LAMB
utterances.text: Your Honours, I would be much obliged if the ushers could convey copies of this summary both to the Bench and to our learned friends.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Will we turn now to cross-examination? Is it Mr. Petrovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. Before I start with my cross-examination, I would like to put a question that has nothing to do with the testimony, but the health condition of my client. The Defence can start the cross-examination immediately; however, our client has complained on several occasions of not feeling too well today. I'm duty-bound to draw your attention to that fact and I would kindly ask the Trial Chamber to either adjourn the cross-examination until tomorrow, or maybe limit the time, so as to enable the accused to return to the conditions where he can relax and rest a little, because in addition to all other problems, he hasn't been able to sleep for nights. I believe that you will have understanding for this request and that you will be able to grant our request.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Petrovic, yes, we'd like you to continue now. There isn't a great deal of time to go in today's session. We'll continue to keep under observation Mr. Strugar, and it may be that a convenient time will come earlier than the normal close of the day when we might break. But if you'd carry on now.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise. Can you give me just a moment. Will the Trial Chamber allow the accused to address the Bench briefly?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Petrovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Already a long time ago I was very clear when I heard what my doctor said, and I informed you of my health condition. In an accident, my vertebra broke in three places. And in addition to that, I, from time to time, regardless of all the drink that I'm taking, I have a problem with coughing. I would have to have some tea to warm me up. I'm been here for days and nobody has been able to provide me with a single cup of tea. I must tell you that this makes me feel very uncomfortable. How is it possible that somebody who is still innocent until proven guilty to be treated like that? Could you please advise those who are looking after my well-being if they cannot provide me with a free cup of tea, I'm perfectly willing to pay. They keep on giving me cold water, which my body will not tolerate. That's one thing. Another thing: I don't know why, but for quite a lot of time now, and my doctor is aware of that, I haven't been able to sleep, and this is nothing new. This is something that I experienced already when I was at the hospital in Belgrade. I was receiving medication, light relaxants, which made me sleep. I would receive half a tablet a night. I continued receiving that; however, I can't sleep. I feel sleepy, Your Honours. I am listening to the witness, but from time to time I doze off, and I really feel embarrassed, thinking that you may notice that I'm dozing off. I may be senile, but I am a proud man. I am a proud human being. So I would kindly ask you either to curtail this testimony or to give me more frequent breaks. This would be all. I'm not asking for any leniency. I know exactly where I am. I'm being tried. But I've been listening to something that I already went through. What happened in Yugoslavia, my defence counsel, I suppose, will be able to tell that. However, was I really -- was it really necessary for me to listen to all that has been said today? What has that got to do with my indictment? Why did I have to listen to all that? So much from me. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I am sure, Mr. Strugar, that it will be possible, and the Chamber now does ask, that arrangements be made for you to be provided with tea, hot tea, during breaks. I don't know why it is that has not been possible until now. If you could take up with the doctor at the Detention Centre your concern about your inability to sleep, I believe it may be possible if some further medication will help, for you to get something extra there. At a time like this, and the stress of an occasion like this, we can certainly understand that your sleep may well be a difficult issue for you, and we can't do anything directly about it. It must be in the hands of the medical people. But I would certainly suggest that you should take that up, and your counsel might reinforce that request by communicating with those in charge of the Detention Centre. The other matter you raised is the evidence. The evidence that's to be tendered here may, I can well understand, appear to you from time to time to have little or nothing to do with what you were doing. A lot of it is in the sense of background and deals with issues that are legal issues, matters of formality, rather than the events on the ground at the time, with which you were directly concerned. But I'm sure that you will come to understand that your counsel and the Prosecution counsel, between them, are watching what matters should be dealt with and what matters should not be dealt with. And if matters that should be dealt with are omitted, then that will be a basis for decision by this Tribunal. So you will understand that counsel must look at those matters carefully. In the case of Mr. Rodic and Mr. Petrovic, they must look at it on your behalf and I'm sure you will be understanding of their continuing efforts on your behalf and will come to understand that if they're accepting certain evidence will be led, nevertheless there's a reason for it, even though you yourself might think it's a waste of everybody's time. We will look at the question of the course of adjournments. It may be possible to arrange for an extra adjournment in the course of an ordinary session by shortening the periods. That may create some problems with the tapes and the recording. I'll make inquiries about that. But perhaps at least getting hot tea will help you in giving you an opportunity to move about during the breaks after that. So thank you. Now, Mr. Petrovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour Cross-examined by. Mr. Petrovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. LAMB
utterances.text: Mrs. Alajbeg, my name is Vladimir Petrovic and I represent General Strugar. I'm going to ask you a few questions about your testimony. Since we speak the same or a similar language, I would kindly ask you to make a break between my question and your answer, since everything is being -- that is being said is being interpreted. Such a break will enable everybody to hear my entire question and your entire answer, which is in our mutual interest. First of all, let me ask you: How did you get in touch with the OTP of the Tribunal in this matter?

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG
utterances.text: As far as I know, representatives of the OTP came in contact with the international legal department, with the Ministry of Foreign Affairs, through their office in Zagreb, and probably they were referred to the department of international affairs in Zagreb. Since after their first contact, they asked somebody to be a witness, somebody who was best informed. Since I was one of the founders of the department for international legal affairs, and probably one of the most senior legal experts in the ministry - all the others joined much later than me - then I was asked to be the one. And one of the things is also that I live in Brussels, so The Hague is close.

utterances.speaker: MS. LAMB
utterances.text: Can I please ask you: Who is it who informed you about the need to testify in front of the Court, and what did they tell you?

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG
utterances.text: Yes. It was the head of the office for cooperation with The Hague Tribunal, Mr. Frane Krnic at the time, and after that, my colleague, who is currently the head of the international legal affairs with the Ministry of Foreign Affairs, Andrea Metelko.

utterances.speaker: MS. LAMB
utterances.text: Can you tell us when that was, approximately?

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG
utterances.text: It was last year, sometime last year.

utterances.speaker: MS. LAMB
utterances.text: When? Towards the end, at the beginning? I'm not asking for any precise dates. Just approximately.

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG
utterances.text: Yes. I'm trying to remember. It was before summer.

utterances.speaker: MS. LAMB
utterances.text: How were you prepared for this testimony?

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG
utterances.text: My colleague, Mrs. Metelko, from the Ministry of Foreign Affairs, told me what would be the interest and what the goal was in order to establish the status of the Republic of Croatia at the time. And since I was aware of a number of those documents that could illustrate that status, obviously I consulted my colleagues in the department, and that's how we were able to pinpoint those documents which might be of interest, and primarily those were international and legal documents, but there were also others.

utterances.speaker: MS. LAMB
utterances.text: Do I understand you correctly what you have just told us is that documents that are in front of us today, the documents that you commented upon today, they are the result of selection by your colleagues in the ministry?

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG
utterances.text: No, not all of the documents, especially not those documents that deal with the internal laws and regulations, primarily those international documents.

utterances.speaker: MS. LAMB
utterances.text: Your colleague, Mrs. Metelko told you that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Could I just ask you to pause a little longer. I've noticed the poor interpreter is rushing hard to keep up.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, as you have just realised, at the beginning of my cross-examination, I drew the witness's attention to this mistake, being aware that I am bound to make it myself. So I would like to apologise for making the mistake.

utterances.speaker: MS. LAMB
utterances.text: You told us that Mrs. Metelko explained to you what the goal of your testimony in front of the International Tribunal would be. What did she tell you?

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG
utterances.text: It was her first and then the OTP representatives told me. And it was exactly like I told you, that the goal would be to establish the status of Croatia at the time. The status of Croatia primarily in the international community or, in other words, the legal state of affairs in Croatia with regard to its international subjectivity, or Croatia being an international subject.

utterances.speaker: MS. LAMB
utterances.text: In addition to the conversations with my learned friends from the OTP, what other contacts have you had from the moment when you were informed that you will be testifying until today, and who were your contacts with?

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG
utterances.text: The only contacts I had were with my colleagues from the international department. I mentioned Mr. Krnic, but soon after that he was replaced by Mr. Jaksa Muljacic, and I spoke with him, and I had contacts with the OTP, and those were my -- all my contacts in that respect.

utterances.speaker: MS. LAMB
utterances.text: Tell me, please: As regards some of the elements of your professional background, in the statement that you gave to the OTP on 19 September, 2003, you say the following: In 1979, you were sent to the federal Ministry of Foreign Affairs by the republican organs. Can you elaborate? Who was it who sent you and what were the circumstances? I'm not prying for any details; just general information.

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG
utterances.text: The federal ministry of international affairs comprised of representatives of various republics and autonomous provinces, and they were -- they joined in various ways. One of the ways of joining was for an adequate body. At that time in Croatia, it was proposed that somebody should go and work in the federal Ministry of Foreign Affairs. And this could be permanent employment or it could be based on a temporary contract. In 1979, I was originally sent by the Executive Council of the parliament of Croatia, and I had a temporary contract, and this was at the request of the federal secretary for internal affairs. They had openings and they dispatched a circular to various republics and they said: We don't have candidates in Belgrade. Can you please send us your candidates. And that's how I was proposed for the post of the consul in Pittsburgh, and later on the advisory in the cultural and information centre. I had a four-year contract to start with.

utterances.speaker: MS. LAMB
utterances.text: To your mind, what was it that qualified you for that position? Because prior to that, you were engaged in commercial law in INA.

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG
utterances.text: I was an advisor in the legal affairs department and I was engaged in legal affairs. I represented my company. I worked on various contracts, investment contracts. I worked on joint ventures. I even drafted some international contracts. There were all sorts of things that I did, legal departments. There were all sorts of things. I was a legal expert with a solid base, a solid knowledge.

utterances.speaker: MS. LAMB
utterances.text: However, the job of a consul and the job in INA, what do they have in common in terms of the character of these two jobs?

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG
utterances.text: There is a lot in common between these two jobs. A consul was supposed to be somebody with a degree in law. They had to be in touch with the profession. They had to be versed in working with judiciary, with governmental bodies, which I did while I worked in INA. For example, I worked on labour law, I worked on all the issues stemming from labour relations, and I also had a bar exam at the time. I was qualified to do this job. This was very important.

utterances.speaker: MS. LAMB
utterances.text: Another thing that comes to mind is the following: I understand that this may be a good explanation. However, how did you become a cultural attache in your next term of office?

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG
utterances.text: No. It was in the same term of office.

utterances.speaker: MS. LAMB
utterances.text: Let's not overlap, please. So in Pittsburgh first you were a consul --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Let the interpreter catch up. She is about half a question behind.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I will put it in front of me in very big letters, and I hope it will remind me every time I speed up.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We'll get a great flag and I'll wave at you when you can start, Mr. Petrovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. LAMB
utterances.text: So what I would like to know: I know what your duties were as a consul. What did you do as a cultural attache? Please can you wait just for a moment. What is a link between a consul and somebody who works as a cultural attache in New York? What are the points in common?

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG
utterances.text: The job in New York lasted for one year. That was my last year of that term of office, which was four years, according to my contract. For three years I was in Pittsburgh, and then I was transferred to the cultural and information centre. I suppose that there were several reasons for that. One of those reasons was that at the time they were downsizing in some diplomatic representative offices, and they assigned people to other places where there were openings. At that moment, in New York, there was an opening. There were two consuls in Pittsburgh and we were told that one of us had to be transferred somewhere else, so it was a good solution that there was an opening in New York, and there was nobody there. There are lots of Croats in the United States, and there was nobody from Croatia to look after their needs. There were other people from other areas but nobody from Croatia. So they thought that it would be good if somebody from Croatia worked in that centre. In addition to that, the post I was assigned to also comprised relations with the diaspora, and although this should not have been one of the tasks; however, I had very large previous experience and they told this would be a really good post for me. Before that, I organised a lot of cultural events in Pittsburgh, and I had a month of culture at that time. This was a big event. So I proved myself as the person who was capable of organising cultural events.

utterances.speaker: MS. LAMB
utterances.text: In addition to some other things, I understand that in the former secretariat for foreign affairs, people were tasked with some categories of emigrants. Croats were in charge of Croats, Serbs in charge of Serbs, Macedonians were in charge of Macedonians.

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG
utterances.text: No, not necessarily. But very often it would happen to me that I would be tasked with Croatian and Slovenian communities, as two communities which share some similar historical developments. However, this was not a rule. We worked with other communities, other ethnic communities. So this was not a steadfast rule. However, it was taken into consideration when thinking about which person in an ethnic community would accept.

utterances.speaker: MS. LAMB
utterances.text: How -- what kind of verification, what kind of checking would a person aspiring to join the secretariat of international affairs would have to undergo? What security checks?

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG
utterances.text: I don't know what security checks I had to be subject to. From time to time, I would bump into a colleague or a friend who would then tell me: Somebody was inquiring, made inquiries about you. And then I realised that this was this check, checking procedure.

utterances.speaker: MS. LAMB
utterances.text: What service was in charge of this checking procedure?

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG
utterances.text: I suppose that this was done through the Ministry of the Interior.

utterances.speaker: MS. LAMB
utterances.text: Do you know more specifically which service within the Ministry of the Interior would be in charge of that?

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG
utterances.text: I really wouldn't know. I wouldn't be able to tell you. At that time, I really don't know who did that.

utterances.speaker: MS. LAMB
utterances.text: Do you know, speaking from the experience working in your ministry, who is it today in Croatia who is in charge of the security checks of the people who are being posted to responsible places abroad?

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG
utterances.text: I believe again that this is the Ministry of the Interior, but I can't tell you exactly who. I know that in 1991, there was a service for the protection of constitutional order. I know that they were the ones who were consulted every time. But at this moment, really, I can't tell you which service that is. I really -- I'm not interested in that.

utterances.speaker: MS. LAMB
utterances.text: Would that be the secret police who would be checking who could work for the Ministry of Foreign Affairs?

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG
utterances.text: This term, "secret service," is something that I really don't understand. Secret police, what does that mean? Is that the security service that used to exist in the past?

utterances.speaker: MS. LAMB
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG
utterances.text: I suppose that that service did have an impact on the checking procedure, but I wouldn't be able to say that for a fact.

utterances.speaker: MS. LAMB
utterances.text: Can we then conclude that you were very successful, that you went successfully through all these checking procedures? Because from a four-year contract, you were given a permanent job.

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG
utterances.text: I can only suppose that all these checking procedures were not successful, like you put it, but I suppose that they were okay. However, when I became a permanent employee, I was again invited through the Executive Council of the Republic of Croatia, when I returned to Croatia, I was still an employee of INA Naftaplin, and I was again invited and they told me that they had a request from the federal secretariat for foreign affairs to send people who had already had some experience with the job and who wished to continue working on those jobs. Because in the federal secretariat for foreign affairs, there was a serious lack of Croatians, and that's the way it was put to me, and that's how I went to Belgrade, and with the then-federal secretary for foreign affairs I had an interview, and he confirmed that he told me that they requested Croatia to send people who would be interested in permanent employment. Those people should have already had some experience, because there was not enough representation of the Republic of Croatia in the federal body.

utterances.speaker: MS. LAMB
utterances.text: Tell me: In the period since you have been involved in foreign affairs - by this, I mean the period of the former Yugoslavia, from 1979 to 1991 - who were the secretaries of foreign affairs, and where were they from, if you can remember? But we all know that.

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG
utterances.text: I think that at that time -- was it Vrhovac? I think it was Vrhovac when I came. Then it was Mojsov. I even think Mojsov was before that. I even think Mojsov was before that, because I know that in New York we prepared some materials for him. And maybe Vrhovac wasn't there any more when I arrived. So it was Mojsov. In the end, it was Loncar. In the meantime --

utterances.speaker: MS. LAMB
utterances.text: Who was there before Loncar?

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG
utterances.text: Well, that's what I'm trying to remember right now. Dizdarevic? Was it him?

utterances.speaker: MS. LAMB
utterances.text: Very well. Let's move on.

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG
utterances.text: I can't really remember at this moment, but I do know that the last minister was Loncar.

utterances.speaker: MS. LAMB
utterances.text: Tell me, please, the following: You returned to the country in 1990?

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG
utterances.text: No. Oh, you mean back to the ministry in Belgrade. You mean that?

utterances.speaker: MS. LAMB
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct then. It was either in December or January. That's when my term of office in Berlin expired.

utterances.speaker: MS. LAMB
utterances.text: Until when did you remain in Belgrade, physically?

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG
utterances.text: Formally --

utterances.speaker: MS. LAMB
utterances.text: I'm asking you about your physical presence.

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG
utterances.text: Well, how can I explain this? Physically, I was in both places at once. It's very unusual, but that's how it was. This was a time of transition, and there were things I still had to do. One of these things was to bring on this care the international treaty base. This was agreed on. It was done in a formal manner. Because the then-republican ministry asked to have a base of an international treaty database and that this should be given to all of us as a kind of common inheritance. However, physically it was hard to do, because the PCs were not adapted.

utterances.speaker: MS. LAMB
utterances.text: I have to interrupt you. I'm asking you something very simple. Until when were you physically present in Belgrade? We'll come to what you were doing, but now I want to know until when you were in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG
utterances.text: Well, I would say -- I repeat that I was in both places, but until the end of November I was there physically. Formally, my employment ended on the 15th of December, but that was because I still had some unused annual leave left and things like that.

utterances.speaker: MS. LAMB
utterances.text: When was the last time you were in Knez Milos Street, where the building of the foreign ministry is? When was the last time you entered as its employee?

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG
utterances.text: Probably to take back my employment booklet.

utterances.speaker: MS. LAMB
utterances.text: And before that?

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG
utterances.text: Well, maybe some 15 days before that, approximately.

utterances.speaker: MS. LAMB
utterances.text: So until the 1st of December you worked in the federal ministry in Belgrade? We are talking about 1991; is that correct? Tell me, please: You say that starting from the spring of 1991, you were in contact with the Ministry of Foreign Affairs of Croatia. Is this correct?

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MS. LAMB
utterances.text: When and how did you establish these contacts, and with whom?

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG
utterances.text: I would that I established contacts even before that, contacts with the first minister of foreign affairs, because I was so-called republican staff member and I felt it was my duty when he was appointed to contact him and to say to him: Well, I am one of these republican civil servants. I have no interest in remaining in a place where you do not need me, and I am prepared to help in any way I can. And then in March, President Tudjman invited all the diplomats in that federal body for a consultation, and quite a lot of us came. The ministry knew about this. This was done quite officially. They knew we had been invited. And we all had a meeting with him, and with the then-representatives of the Croatian Ministry of Foreign Affairs. This was in the spring of 1991, when we were told that we were expected to be working in the interests of Croatia, which had sent us there, and to remain where we were until the circumstances were created for those of us who wished to, to return to Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MS. LAMB
utterances.text: What did the president tell you on that occasion the interests of Croatia were, in the spring of 1991?

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG
utterances.text: He certainly told us that it was in our interest to have our own sovereignty and that, in future, we would see whether we would enter into some kind of community of independent states or in some other way, but at any rate, that at that moment that was the goal of the Republic of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MS. LAMB
utterances.text: So you went to Belgrade to work in a federal body with an aim that was anticonstitutional in relation to the then-existing state?

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG
utterances.text: No, because at that time it was very well known that Croatia had already enacted its own constitution and had, by promulgating this constitution, declared its desire for independence. And it was also very well known that we, as republican civil servants -- and this was a very difficult thing to understand in times of transition. At that time some colleagues who came to be prepared for assignments abroad spoke quite openly in the Ministry of Foreign Affairs, in all the departments, that they would advocate the interests of the Republic of Croatia. And this was public knowledge.

utterances.speaker: MS. LAMB
utterances.text: Could you please be more concise in your replies, if possible, because I get lost and repeat my questions, and we are wasting our precious time, mine and yours and the Court's. From the viewpoint of the federal constitution that was then in force, was the secession of the Republic of Croatia, such as you were instructed about from the president of Croatia at the time, was this a goal that was opposed to the then-valid constitution of the SFRY or not?

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG
utterances.text: It's impossible to answer this with a yes or no, because at that time we did not feel we were working against the constitution or the system of the then-Yugoslavia. It was simply something that was complementary to that.

utterances.speaker: MS. LAMB
utterances.text: The constitution of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, did it contain the categories of secession? I'm speaking of the Socialist Federative Republic of Yugoslavia. Was secession, disassociation, or anything similar, provided for in that constitution?

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG
utterances.text: Yes. In the preamble to both the federal and the republican constitutions, it said that the republics had to join together voluntarily on the basis of their right to self-determination, including the right to secession.

utterances.speaker: MS. LAMB
utterances.text: In the text of the constitution, was there a provision defining a procedure for any republic to secede from the Socialist Federative Republic of Yugoslavia? What article was this?

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG
utterances.text: No. There was no such article, but there was no -- nothing to prohibit it either. It was simply a gap in the constitution.

utterances.speaker: MS. LAMB
utterances.text: Does this constitution contain an unambiguous provision which states that any changes of the borders of the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia could not be made without the consent of all the federal units of that state?

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG
utterances.text: We have to know that the Republic of Croatia did work on its independence as a legal entity in international law, but at that time it was not certain that the republic wished full independence. It was possibly heading for a confederation, and this was well known. Croatia and Slovenia advocated a confederation at the time.

utterances.speaker: MS. LAMB
utterances.text: I have to ask you to answer my question. Is there a prohibition in the constitution for the change of the borders of the state without everybody's consent? Yes or no.

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG
utterances.text: There was no change of borders in this case.

utterances.speaker: MS. LAMB
utterances.text: Please. If there is a state, and if there are five states there today, how, then, can we say that there were no changes in the borders? Do you understand that? I'm sure you understand my question, so please answer it.

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG
utterances.text: I know what you're getting at. I know what you want me to say. But at that time, Croatia had not declared independence, nor did Croatia at that time secede from Yugoslavia. So we can in no way speak about changing the borders. We can only talk about an order in which Croatia has its own sovereignty. We know that the characteristics of sovereignty was something that the former republics had.

utterances.speaker: MS. LAMB
utterances.text: Does the constitution contain the prohibition or not?

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG
utterances.text: Prohibition of what?

utterances.speaker: MS. LAMB
utterances.text: A prohibition of a forcible change of borders of the SFRY, without the consent of the constituent elements of that state; yes or no?

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG
utterances.text: Forcible change? I really can't tell you what article refers to a forcible change. But I repeat: At that time, in no way was any change of borders in question.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I have to apply to you for assistance. I'm asking something very simple: Did the constitution contain such a provision or not? Or does the witness not know this? These are three possibilities. I would like to receive a simple answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I wonder if you could assist us there with that. I think you have a reasonable familiarity with the constitution, and I do not have that familiarity. But I would be surprised to find in a federal constitution that there was a provision that expressly contemplated the dissolution or breaking up of the federation. Is there such a provision in the -- or was there such a provision in the federal constitution at that time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] A provision on the dissolution of the state did not exist.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] By your leave: Was there a provision on changing the borders without the consent of the federal units?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Border changes. Was there any provision dealing with that, do you think?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Of the federal state.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As far as I know, the provision on changing of borders between the republics existed, because the republics would have to agree on that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: You understand the point of Mr. Petrovic's question, which is directed to the federal borders, that is, the external border of the Federation. Was there any provision dealing with that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Apart from the general principle that the borders were inviolable, I cannot quote any other provision as regards the external borders.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I think we can take the answer, Mr. Petrovic, to be no.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, of course, when the time comes, we shall adduce evidence to that effect. Just a moment, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. LAMB
utterances.text: Does the fact that you don't know the answer to the question I put to you have anything to do with the instructions you were given when you came to this institution?

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG
utterances.text: What institution are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: MS. LAMB
utterances.text: The International Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG
utterances.text: No. I told you that I did not consult anyone, especially not any other experts, apart from the people I've mentioned, and certainly not with people who are not lawyers.

utterances.speaker: MS. LAMB
utterances.text: Were you ever a member of the League of Communists of Croatia or of Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG
utterances.text: Yes, long ago, and then we simply all stopped being members. I can't tell you exactly when.

utterances.speaker: MS. LAMB
utterances.text: When did you enter the Communist Party?

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG
utterances.text: At the time, it was called the League of Communists of Yugoslavia, and more specifically, of the Republic of Croatia, and that was when we were students, either at university or school.

utterances.speaker: MS. LAMB
utterances.text: Until when were you a member of the League of Communists of Yugoslavia and Croatia?

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG
utterances.text: This was up to the '80s, as far as I can remember, when all of us stopped paying our membership dues. That was somewhere in the '80s.

utterances.speaker: MS. LAMB
utterances.text: Can you give me a specific date?

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG
utterances.text: No, because I didn't formally ask to cease being a member. I simply stopped paying my membership dues, and this was sometime in the '80s.

utterances.speaker: MS. LAMB
utterances.text: The late '80s?

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. LAMB
utterances.text: For how long were you a member of the League of Communists?

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG
utterances.text: Well, from the '60s to the '80s, so it might have been about 25 years or so. But I wish to mention that I never held any posts in that league.

utterances.speaker: MS. LAMB
utterances.text: Were you also within the communist organisation of the Ministry of Foreign Affairs?

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG
utterances.text: We all were, but I didn't have any special function.

utterances.speaker: MS. LAMB
utterances.text: Were you ever disciplined as a party member?

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG
utterances.text: No, I wasn't.

utterances.speaker: MS. LAMB
utterances.text: After being a member of that party, did you join any other party?

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. LAMB
utterances.text: Are you a member of a political party today?

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG
utterances.text: No, I'm not.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, in view of the fact that I have completed one topic, I propose that we conclude for today, by your leave.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Petrovic, I think that's a convenient time. I must ask, Mrs. Alajbeg, if you can return tomorrow. I'm sorry about that. That will be at 9.00 in the morning.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honour. I'm sorry to interrupt you before you conclude. I just want I thought it might be helpful since a day or two have passed to remind the Chamber that Mrs. Alajbeg does have to leave The Hague tomorrow afternoon, that she is not able to stay beyond tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We're in the hands of Mr. Petrovic there. I'm sure that he's moving on now, and we can hope to finish in time for you to get away.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I will do my very best. But this depends to a certain extent on the way in which my conversation with the witness proceeds tomorrow. I will focus on only key issues. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I think that will be very useful, if you could do that, Mr. Petrovic, and we're starting to get into a pattern now of allowing question and answer to be concluded so that the interpreters can keep up, and overall, that will speed up the process as well. We will adjourn now until tomorrow morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: To be reconvened on Friday, the 16th day of January 2004, at 9.00 a.m. 19 20 21 22 23 24 25

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 1.37 p.m.
